articles.title: Unions Step Up to Meet the Moment
articles.content: Featured image by Jared Rodriguez Since taking office, Trump and MAGA forces have made considerable advances in implementing Project 2025 and consolidating authoritarian power—but many of these moves have proved unpopular and undermined their support. With Trump’s approval ratings dropping and elements of his coalition defecting, conditions look promising for pushing back MAGA in the midterm elections. But there are at least two sources of concern. With their support declining, the MAGA forces are likely to step up their efforts to interfere with the elections—doing everything from stopping people from voting to refusing to seat elected officials to unleashing violence. And even if elections go smoothly, will the anti-MAGA forces be prepared to govern in a way that brings about real change? Or will we face business-as-usual Democrats who answer to billionaires and waffle on key reforms? A growing number of billionaires support authoritarian rule because they directly benefit from it or know they could not amass such wealth under a true democracy. Labor unions can play a crucial role on both fronts. When unions are engaged in democracy movements, the odds of defeating authoritarian rule increase, according to political scientists who examined cases of democratic backsliding. This moment calls for unions to step up to defend against MAGA attacks and guard the gains of working people. But we’ve never had real democracy in this country; it is also a time to go on offense, and fight for a true, expansive and inclusive democracy. We need bold union leadership to block authoritarianism and build real democracy. So what are unions doing to meet the moment? A handful of locals have been leading by example for at least a decade, including the Chicago Teachers Union , SEIU Local 26 in Minnesota, and the United Teachers of Los Angeles . Those unions provide excellent lessons on how to build internal power and long-term strategy, putting them in strong shape to meet the moment. In this article I share lessons from a handful of other unions, as well as May Day Strong –a national coalition of unions, community organizations, faith groups and others working to build power to block authoritarian and billionaire attacks and build a progressive movement for multiracial democracy. Perhaps the union that has taken the boldest steps towards a comprehensive strategy is the National Nurses United (NNU). Under the leadership of a new Executive Director, Puneet Maharaj, the NNU has undertaken a rigorous planning process to develop strategies for defense and offense. The union came up with their “ Vision for a Healthy Society ,” a 10-point program that puts patients, nurses, communities and the planet over profit. The Vision is a long-term agenda . Its bold, expansive demands, such as the right to health and freedom from corporate domination, can’t likely be won in the next few years; they will take power building and stepping-stone fights to achieve. But this vision anchors NNU’s work so that nurses know what they are fighting for , not just what they are fighting against . While they develop leaders and build capacity for winning the long-term vision, the union is also fighting to block authoritarianism. They’ve developed new educational materials and social media to teach members about authoritarianism and the unique role unions and nurses have to play in this moment. NNU is not shying away from the fight, noting: “Unions have a long, successful history of defeating fascism. The Trump administration’s actions over the past 15 months have made it clear: It’s time to take up the mantle again.” They’ve created Nurses for Democracy to engage more members in voter turnout and election defense, and to be ready to push for their bold vision. The program involves political education and civil disobedience training. This summer, nurses from around the country met in Chicago to get trained in non-cooperation and de-escalation, and to dive deeper into scenarios for election defense this fall. NNU’s democracy defense also includes spirited offense against the corporations that are enabling and profiting off of the authoritarian regime. The union is taking on Palantir for a number of reasons. First, Palantir directly supports authoritarian leaders and practices by providing surveillance technology and systems used in immigration enforcement and in Gaza and elsewhere. The company has been moving into the healthcare system, and now its software is being used for nurse scheduling, replacing humans who can assure safe staffing ratios. Working with the Purge Palantir coalition, NNU has been protesting at a number of sites, demanding politicians return Palantir donations and that HCA Healthcare drop their use of Palantir software. They held a national day of action against Palantir on August 27 , and plan to join an international action in late September. As part of their fightback against fascism, NNU has recently rolled out a “Red Line Pledge” campaign, with a goal of having one-on-one conversations with 75 percent of their membership to assess their readiness to take action to protect patients, the union, and democracy in the event of subverted elections or other red lines being crossed. Members will be asked to sign pledge cards (CARD PASTED BELOW). Finally, NNU knows it can’t win the defensive or offensive fights on their own. No union or organization is powerful enough to do that, and so they must work within a united front. To that end the NNU has stepped up its engagement with May Day Strong.. Nurses helped organize May Day 2026 actions, and NNU representatives play an active role in May Day Strong committees. The National Education Association has also taken steps to meet the moment. The union has argued that attacks on education are attacks on democracy, and vice versa. The NEA has invested staff and resources in helping state and local affiliates organize to defend democracy and public education. The union is taking on the billionaire class through its support for Tax the Rich campaigns. The Massachusetts Teachers Association (MTA) led the way with its Fair Share amendment, which raised taxes by four percent on income above one million dollars. Passed by voters in 2022, the tax has been a huge success, bringing in billions of dollars with no evidence of wealthy people leaving the state. Max Page, president of the MTA at the time Fair Share was passed, is working with affiliates around the country to pass similar measures and the NEA has set aside resources to support 19 Tax the Rich campaigns around the country. These campaigns take a variety of forms. For example, the Vermont NEA affiliate is helping to lead the Fair Share for Vermont campaign, which would create a new tax bracket for the top one percent of Vermont taxpayers. NEA is also an active participant in May Day Strong. They’ve sent hundreds of member leaders to national May Day Strong convenings, including seasoned leaders and newer activist members. In 2026, the NEA helped anchor over 1,000 May Day actions around the country. In North Carolina, anticipating significant educator participation in the “Kids Over Billionaires” action, at least 22 school districts across the state decided to close for the day. The 2026 summer meeting of the National Council of Urban Education Associations, an independent body representing the interests of NEA’s local affiliates, featured a panel discussion highlighting the ways NEA locals are resisting authoritarianism and defending student rights. Union leaders from St. Paul, Minnesota, Pueblo, Colorado, and Lee County, Florida shared the work they’ve been doing to fight ICE, resist union busting and censorship, and move from servicing to organizing. Union leaders stressed repeatedly the urgency of the moment and the existential threat facing our educators and schools. At the same time, they were clear that defending against attacks isn’t enough: we need to stay focused on a vision of schools that our students and educators deserve. The Philadelphia AFL-CIO Central Labor Council (CLC), and UNITE HERE Local 274 used May Day 2025 as an opportunity to build new relationships between unions and community organizations. UNITE HERE 274, which represents private-sector hotel and food service workers, has been punching above its weight for a while now. The union knows how to organize workers and win strong contracts. They are not afraid to strike, and they have members who are highly engaged and skilled in leading workplace actions. And the local has played a pivotal role in electoral politics in recent years. But President Rosslyn Wuchinich knew that this moment calls for even more. Fighting authoritarianism and making multiracial democracy real will require the local stepping into new strategies. Wuchinich has worked with new Philadelphia CLC leaders to pull together a coalition—Workers Over Billionaires—comprised of labor unions, faith and community allies ready to do more. The CLC’s Chief of Staff, Jana Korn, has functioned as the organizer of the group, and the CLC’s organizing director and communications director are also providing support to locals. Last May Day, they organized a rally with Bernie Sanders that drew a huge crowd under the banner “Workers Over Billionaires.” But in an even more significant event, the elected leaders of UNITE HERE 274, the CLC, AFSCME District Council 33, AFSCME District Council 47, AFGE District 3, and Teamsters 623 led a large group blocking one of the city’s major freeway entrances. Those leaders, along with 70 other labor, community and faith members and leaders, got arrested together. The event built new relationships and trust, and marked the first time in decades the labor council organized mass civil disobedience. From there, Workers Over Billionaires knew they needed to dig in deeper. They began by pulling together elected leaders and getting agreement that they needed to be able to speak in a unified voice around a broader agenda, and that the unions had to make a real commitment to engage their members. This meant the union could not just show up as a spokesperson to a meeting or events, but had to bring this program back into their membership. A lot of unions might be able to mobilize around a contract fight but can they engage members around a broader agenda? Wuchinich says, “the work inside of your own membership is the most important thing.” Members had to get engaged in order for this program to work. In December 2025 they brought together about 80 staff from unions and allied community organizations for a two-day workshop and training to build relationships, a sense of shared purpose, and trust. They used exercises to develop shared values and then laid out the arc of a campaign timeline. The training included developing a rap to use in organizing conversations with members. Between January and March, they went to their members and asked: What are the biggest challenges facing you, your community, your coworkers, and your family? What keeps you up at night? If you and your family, your co-workers, and your community were in charge, what would you do differently? They used these answers to begin to build a working-class agenda for Philadelphia. In March they brought together 300 worker leaders for a two-hour event to preview the agenda. People read off parts of the statement and spoke about the meaning of the proposal in their own life and work. On May Day 2026 they held an event to ratify the working-class agenda, with large banners representing different planks of the agenda, and a sign reading, “The next 250 years are for us.” Different groups spoke to different elements of the agenda and different campaigns, but it all felt cohesive and part of one united movement. “I think we in unions really underestimate how important it is for people to be together,” Wuchinich said. “It pays massive dividends, to just get people in a space with people from other unions and community groups and feel part of something much bigger than just their own organization.” You can talk to people about a big vision but actually being there together is what makes it real. And building the long-term vision allowed people to see how their fights are connected. “We’re all endorsing this much broader agenda, and we might be taking leadership more specifically on one or two pieces of that ourselves, but we all see it as one thing, it’s all necessary. We all need all of these things,” she said. In the afternoon, they held a rally with about 5,000 people. Most encouraging was the fact that many people were there with organizations, reflecting serious progress in groups doing intentional turnout. The group marched past various corporate targets, including many that were employers the unions or community were fighting, including the Sheraton hotel where UNITE HERE members were picketing. The police tried to block the crowd from entering the private driveway but the crowd remained strong, chanting, “Let us through!” until the police eventually gave up. “Our members were on fire. It was electric and a huge shot in the arm too, for those workers haven’t won their contract yet,” said Wuchinich. The process has been incredibly successful in terms of bringing together labor and community in a unified voice on a broader agenda“It is historic in this city. I can confidently say, we’ve never seen anything like this this century in Philadelphia,”she said. The second goal, getting more unions to do deeper internal organizing within their membership, has had mixed results. For some unions, this is a new skill or one that hasn’t been flexed in a long time. But several are working hard at it, and it helps that the program is running through the CLC and can provide some resources. Other unions do have a practice of internal organizing and do it regularly, so they faced the challenge of connecting that ongoing work with this broader alignment effort. The best case is to tie these things together, so when organizers talk to their members they are engaging them on both fronts (the short-term contract fight and the long-term agenda). More unions and community organizations have gotten involved in Workers Over Billionaires since last year, among them AFSCME DC47. The council represents nine locals, two of the largest representing technical and administrative employees for the city of Philadelphia. But beyond that, their members include workers at the zoo, many of the museums and more. DC47 has been growing. And according to Robert Harris, the vice president, and political and legislative director, this has created a virtuous circle: new organizing brings in new members who want to see their union move into more organizing, which in turns pushes the council from a service model to an organizing model. Many of these new members, Harris said, see the union as not only giving them a voice on the worksite, but also a base for “fighting for democracy in the city of Philadelphia, and in the state of Pennsylvania, and beyond.” DC47 began to work with the CLC, UNITE HERE 274 and a few other unions in the 2023 mayoral election. This built relationships among union leaders, and laid the groundwork to deepen the coalition-building and develop internal organizing conversations. The council brought leaders to the three-day training run by the coalition. And some other members attended a one-day Saturday training at the union hall. Harris is honest about the challenges. While a lot of members were excited and enjoyed the training, many didn’t follow through with the commitment to go back to their worksites and organize 10 co-workers. Some of the members that attended the training are active in progressive groups and were possibly reluctant to intermingle those priorities with this worksite organizing agenda. Or it might be that the “workers over billionaires” frame isn’t resonating, or they are not yet able to connect workplace power with broader fights. And for some, it is a new muscle to build and will take time. Harris knows they need to keep providing education and connecting the dots for their membership, and making the case that working in coalition gives workers a stronger voice. Since May Day 2026, the groups have hosted a week of action leading up to July 4th and World Cup games and are now figuring out next steps, with an eye to a possible focus on election defense. But the group will continue to work on their long-term Working Class Agenda which unites them around a positive vision. Many of the unions profiled here are active in May Day Strong . The coalition began testing its muscle by hosting May Day and Labor Day actions around the country in 2025. They then launched Solidarity Schools, which brought together leaders and members to learn political economy and organizing skills, such as building strong alignments and developing shared campaigns. After hosting more than 5,000 actions on May Day 2026, the network has turned its attention to building the power to disrupt business as usual if necessary this fall, preparing for economic noncooperation in case of an acute election steal.. They are hosting webinar trainings and Solidarity Schools around the country to prepare. They’ve also launched a corporate strategy to pull out the corporate pillar supporting authoritarianism, which includes canvassing in neighborhoods to get small business to sign onto the Business for Democracy Pledge while putting street heat on some of the bigger corporate players aligned with the administration, But the network knows it can’t just focus on elections; it must also help organizations be ready to push forward a bold affordability agenda coming out of the midterms. Like the unions profiled here, they know that the fight can’t just stop with elections and blocking the right.May Day Strong is working with movement allies to develop a freedom charter to unveil in 2027. An effective movement against authoritarianism must also build the progressive forces needed to bring in the world that we deserve.

articles.title: Billy Evans’s You Can See Everything Deal Is the Real Story
articles.author: Stephen Lurie
articles.content: In just over a month in theaters, the new A24 film from Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim has grossed over $93 million at the domestic box office, more than twelve times its $7 million budget. Had things gone as originally planned, a meaningful share of that money would now be flowing to Billy Evans — Elizabeth Holmes’s partner and the film’s de facto antagonist — under the profit-sharing deal he negotiated on camera in exchange for the couple’s participation. Evans has since told CBS News that his share would have been worth tens of millions of dollars. We came close to living in that timeline: one in which moviegoers became, without knowing it, funders of the man now running what he himself dubs a “Theranos 2.0,” his blood-testing startup, Haemanthus. We have Evans — or Evans and A24 — to thank that we don’t. A title card at the end of the film tells us he “relinquished his negotiated share of the film’s profits and would not receive backend compensation.” That turns out to be incomplete. The Hollywood Reporter ( THR ) has since reported, citing two sources, that Evans’s representatives negotiated for that share to be paid out after all — to an unnamed children’s charity. At a Q&A last weekend, the directors disputed THR ’s framing and, according to Semafor , said none of the film’s subjects were paid; a studio source told Semafor that Evans and A24 agreed to send the proceeds to charity, with Evans giving up his own participation as part of the arrangement. Neither the charity nor the amount has been disclosed. THR ’s editor in chief, Maer Roshan, told Semafor the outlet stands by its reporting, calling A24's position “a pretty semantic argument.” Either way, money owed under the deal is leaving the film’s coffers — just not for Evans’s pocket. What we do know is that A24 and the directors initially agreed to pay Evans a portion of the proceeds, that everything we see on-screen was produced under the auspices of that deal, and that there’s no reason to believe they would have backed out of it themselves. In this light, alongside the critical appreciation the film has earned for its transcendent creativity and virtuosity, You Can See Everything should also be understood as something both more base and familiar: a deception practiced on its audience — a fraud in all but the legal sense. And as a wildly successful one, it may also push documentary filmmaking, as a whole, further toward crisis. The film is seemingly transparent about the compromise at its foundation. From what’s shown on screen, we can conclude that the filmmakers, the studio, and Evans agreed — with or without Holmes’s knowledge — to make a film where at least one core subject would be paid in proportion to its earnings, while the film would be sold to the public as vérité documentary. That is what we see in the first half of the film. The arrangement unravels only when Holmes casually mentions to Fielder that she isn’t participating for money, raising the possibility that Evans had cut her out of the deal. It is entirely reasonable to suspect that had this discrepancy remained quiet — rather than metastasizing into the film’s second act — none of the parties would have disclosed the compensation agreement to the public. “Pay-to-Play” Documentaries Are Becoming the Norm What complicates matters is that arrangements like this have become commonplace. As Evans himself argues, documentary subjects are sometimes now paid for their participation — though invoking Harry and Meghan’s $100 million deal with Netflix was probably not the most persuasive benchmark for his negotiations. This phenomenon is an outgrowth of the genre’s ascendance in the streaming era. As streamers recognized how cheap documentaries are to produce and latched onto growing demand, the genre exploded — and is expected to continue to grow. Commercialization set off a competition for subjects, and the subjects, in turn, gained unprecedented leverage for money and control. Crime documentaries and other fare about unsavory characters, which have increasingly dominated the streaming space, are no exception. Fyre Festival founder Billy McFarland shopped his participation to dueling productions from Netflix and Hulu — Netflix declined to pay him, but Hulu paid . Amazon MGM paid a reported $40 million to license Melania , and Donald Trump himself reported a $10.7 million licensing fee from the film on his financial disclosure. Most ordinary people receive no money for their appearance on reality TV, while some high-profile cast members, like those on the Real Housewives franchises, reportedly earn hundreds of thousands of dollars or more per season. There is enormous public demand to watch bad people doing bad things. And while paying subjects remains controversial among documentarians — some prominent directors and studios maintain their own opposition to the practice — it is neither illegal nor barred by Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences eligibility rules for awards, nor is disclosure of such payment required by documentary festivals. In this sense, You Can See Everything sits closer to the center of current documentary trends than to the margins: it has celebrity, crime, and a production team ready to cross all kinds of norms to get the story. But even if the film fits in, its attempted profit-sharing scheme should still stand out. Many celebrity-driven documentaries are open about their subjects’ financial stakes, often crediting them as producers. Here A24 would have every incentive to keep quiet about this deal, with this recipient, and in a film about this subject matter. Public knowledge that proceeds would be going into Evans’s pocket could have crushed enthusiasm for the opening; moviegoers out to witness a retrospective on a scam would instead be unwitting investors in the subjects’ current venture. That the money is now bound for a children’s charity rather than Evans doesn’t mean the attempt carries no consequences. After all, conspiracy to commit fraud on investors — one of Holmes’s four convictions — does not require successful completion of the fraud. Plenty of other damage can be done by the attempt alone. The Rise of Billy Evans Everyone involved in the attempt will benefit from the effort. Billy Evans, despite his unsavoriness, has been granted a stratospheric rise in publicity. Our attentional economy will allow him to leverage this attention into power, at the very least among his fellow aggrieved, right-wing tech bros. With critical and financial success and talk of becoming the first documentary to be nominated for the Best Picture Oscar, Fielder and Oppenheim have made the jump from cult favorites to top-tier stars. A24 cements its status as a studio capable of commanding national attention. But most consequentially, perhaps, Elizabeth Holmes has received an astonishing rehabilitation courtesy of a sympathetic portrait that elides the Holmes described in prosecutors’ filings outlining the full extent of her crimes , and in the many accounts of the darker side of her character. Where does that leave the audience? Aesthetically, we are rewarded. Calling the film a kind of fraud does not contradict its excellence as art: rather, the fusion of its subject matter and form underscores its slipperiness. That slipperiness is essential to its success, both exploring and embodying our modern fascination with the scam. The film enters the glut of podcasts, books, television shows, and movies about scams, frauds, and crimes of this millennium and then jumps to another dimension. The traditional structure of this genre is a reconstruction of a magic trick: we saw the result, and now we get to learn the methods of our deception. You Can See Everything is yet another illusion presented as the reveal. Judging by the pleasure, debate, and thought the film has provoked, viewers absorb this duplicity — we are both the mark of the scam and included as a beneficiary. But if we are to judge You Can See Everything as a documentary — which the makers insist we do — artistry isn’t enough. Truth matters, too. A generous defense of the filmmakers would be that they believed moviegoers would have prior knowledge sufficient to engage the material from a responsible perspective. But presenting a misleading narrative — say, that the crux of Holmes’s innocence is whether “can” really meant “eventually capable of” — is not acceptable simply because facts elsewhere demonstrate her guilt was far broader. Moreover, as we know from many other stunning documentaries, truth and drama are plenty compatible. In fact, both could have been harmonized quite easily here, too. On a recent episode of the podcast Search Engine , host PJ Vogt and Theranos whistleblower Tyler Shultz discuss the chasm between the representation of Holmes on screen and reality — and how the public has fallen into it. They ask why the film couldn’t have a coda that put the artistic experience in its proper context, something like a supercut of Holmes’s many lies and wrongs. To disclose such a reality after the film has so successfully worked its magic, after Holmes has charmed Fielder and Fielder has charmed us, would only make the film’s effect even more powerful. The filmmakers and studio must have discussed and rejected this option, choosing instead an epilogue that reveals Evans had given up his share — while leaving out that, it now appears, the share is being paid to charity. Viewers should wonder why. Perhaps, given the intimacy granted to them by the financial arrangement, they wanted to provide a sympathetic vision of Holmes. Or perhaps they just didn’t feel that genuine representation was their responsibility. Neither seems like a good precedent for documentary filmmaking. We may have missed the timeline in which moviegoers paid Billy Evans millions of dollars, but the popularity and acclaim of You Can See Everything may carry other costs. What does it mean for the most successful nonmusical documentary of the decade to be made under a financial arrangement with its subject and to value story over reality? It could force a needed reckoning with the financialization of the genre. More likely, it will push the field further away from journalistic norms. A lesser production might have been widely condemned for its complicity, but Fielder and Oppenheim have faced no concerted backlash from critics or peers. There will apparently be no consequences for the pay-to-play arrangement that made this film possible and made it what it is. With enough charm, they seem to have learned, you really can get away with anything. articles.title: Rikers Island Set To Close in 2032 & SRG To Be Disbanded
articles.author: The Thorn - NYC DSA Electoral Working Group
articles.content: Local News In a video collaboration with New York City Councilmember Chi Osse (Council District 36, Bedford–Stuyvesant), Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced the official disbandment of the NYPD’s Strategic Response Group (SRG), addressing a campaign promise to separate protest response from counterterrorism functions. The SRG will be replaced with a civilian-led Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division (CDDD), and the NYPD’s protest response will be through a specialized dialogue team, named the First Amendment Support Team (FAST). Rikers Island—notorious for its overcrowding, inmate/correctional violence, and egregious living conditions— is set to shut its doors in 2032 . In place of Rikers Island will be four borough jails opening between 2029 and 2032, and the overall inmate population is intended to be reduced from 6,700 to approximately 4,000. Mayor Mamdani signed Romanch’s Law , officially banning horse-drawn carriages , effective June 2028. Per the Pied-à-Terre tax, 7,489 homes in New York City were collectively billed over $563 million . Amazon has been pushing in-app warnings against the New York City Council’s Intro 518, or the Delivery Protection Act , claiming the legislation “could increase fees for New Yorkers by up to $5.00 per order.” The International Brotherhood of Teamsters and Mayor Mamdani support the bill. The MTA proposed fare hikes for the subway, buses, Long Island Rail Road, and Metro-North in 2027. Additionally, congestion pricing is also set to increase in 2028. New York Attorney General Letitia James unveiled the AI Safety Enforcement Unit , which aims to address data privacy risks and chatbots manipulating children. Election News Congressman Hakeem Jeffries (NY-8) is expected to become the first Black Speaker of the United States House of Representatives, with 251 House Democrats voting in favor of proposing him. 11 Democrats, however, voted against his nomination. Two nays came from incoming Congresswomen Claire Valdez (NY-7) and Daraliaza Avila Chevalier (NY-13). A joint statement with them and five other progressive members was released , addressing work needed to be done for Hakeem Jeffries to combat ICE terror, the Iran War, ending the genocide in Gaza, and supporting Medicare for All.

articles.title: Chicago DSA Should Invest in Childcare as an Organizing Skill
articles.author: Midwestern Socialist -- Chicago DSA
articles.content: Caregivers looking after children of any age, but especially young ones, must offer proper nourishment and hydration, mental clarity, flexibility, a sense of joy, a sense of safety, and the ability to communicate clearly. Many of the skills that childcare requires overlap with the skills that make good organizers. If we, as socialists and as a growing political organization in the city of Chicago, want to expand our reach, we need to grow our childcare operation. If we want to fight for a better future for our children, and that includes the children of our members, we have to build structures to take care of them now. As our organization develops, acquires new office space in different areas of the city, expands meetings, and onboards new members, integrating our membership into our Child Watch program should be key to new member’s introduction to the chapter. I’ve been doing Child Watch at General Chapter Meetings and Endorsement forums for the past year. At my first general meeting, a little overwhelmed and distracted by all the new terms and processes, I heard the noises of kids coming from another room. As a doula and former nanny, I immediately wished I could just be in that room with the kids instead of trying to figure out how I should vote. Soon I found myself in the childcare room, but also increasingly motivated to balance my participation in our highest chapter decision-making body with my responsibility to our member’s children. As it stands, there is a small pool of Child Watch volunteers who work with the GCM subcommittee to make this care happen for every meeting. We hang out with the kids, chase after the toddlers, do arts and crafts, and talk with the older children. We bring them in at the end to sing Solidarity Forever (if they don’t need to go home for naptime before the meeting is over). When there’s a vote or debate on something one of our volunteers really values, we cover for each other to be able to go in and support what we care about. Oftentimes, we all discuss the resolutions together and then vote on Zoom from the child room. Child Watch gives members an opportunity to participate in our large meetings, meet people they might not organize with otherwise, and connect with the parents of our socialist future. It should not be dependent on a small group of organizers, who are, of course, mostly women and parents, to put on for every meeting. It is a valuable skill to be able to be present with children, and it strengthens our organization to allow parents to be present as members while still prioritizing the needs of their children through communication with the Child Watch volunteers. How can we grow this program For members without formal experience with children, the Child Watch program can produce a guide and opportunities for training to get people prepared to help. Specifically, we may choose to require CPR training and a basic conversation for first-time volunteers about child safety, as well as “do’s” and “dont’s” of working with children, group management of multiple ages, and parent communication. Many of our members are educators, and most understandably want a break from the day job when they come to meetings. However, since the skill set exists already within our chapter, it is our job to tap into it and to convince our membership that it is an advantage and a gift to care for each other as we make decisions and prioritize in-person, democratic processes. A little effort goes a long way. We have so much to learn from each other, and our General Chapter Meetings are a great place to meet comrades organizing in other parts of the city and doing different types of committee work. Child Watch is a great place for this to happen, and can become a hub for our members connecting across disciplines within our chapter. Once members train and participate in Child Watch at a General Chapter Meeting, they should be empowered to take those skills back to their committees and events, and encouraged to plan and execute Child Watch at larger in-person meetings on a case-by-case basis. In order to create these spaces for debate and ensure that all members can be included in the conversation, we need to prioritize the skill of childcare so that parents curious about our work and just getting into socialist organizing will feel welcomed and comfortable coming as they are. Participating in Child Watch is also a low barrier to entry for new members to learn how our chapter functions, giving them concrete tasks to do that can help them to plug into how our chapter functions. I am a firm believer that lifting the curtain on how our chapter works can empower our members to help make it happen, spread the load and make the lift of organizing our membership easier. The post Chicago DSA Should Invest in Childcare as an Organizing Skill appeared first on Midwest Socialist .

articles.title: Arlington Police Used a Drone and Undercover Officer to Surveil and Photograph Pro-Palestine Protesters
articles.author: Working Mass: The Massachusetts DSA Labor Outlet
articles.content: The APD drone, above the protest on September 8 (Working Mass) By: Avi R ARLINGTON – The Arlington Police Department (APD), based in a suburb of Boston, escalated to the use of a drone to surveil a small protest in September. The drone was donated by the Arlington Rotary Club, bypassing town oversight . Arlington Police Department (APD) guidelines for drone usage are broad and do little to prevent the surveillance of protests and public gatherings. When questioned, multiple APD officials encouraged people to rely on the “positive intentions” of the police officers, but drone deployment records and local activists raise concerns around privacy and surveillance. Where will lines be drawn and how will the public know? Is this the new normal in Arlington and in police departments, big and small, across the United States? The September Protest Against Rep. Katherine Clark On Tuesday, September 8, around 30 pro-Palestine activists gathered outside Arlington Town Hall to protest Representative Katherine Clark’s presence at the the Union of Concerned Scientist’s (UCS) forum. The activists had called on UCS, a non-profit focused on using scientific research to improve global health, safety, and sustainability, to disinvite Clark from the panel due to her votes to fund and send weapons to Israel’s military during the ecocide and genocide in Gaza. Clark is the House Minority Whip and the second most powerful Democrat in Congress. She has received close to $1 million from AIPAC. The protest was co-organized by a number of local groups, including Arlington for Palestine, Boston Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), and others. The activists gathered with signs around the steps of Arlington Town Hall to chant, speak in front of a local news outlet, and hand out information to pedestrians and attendees. Their message was centered around the contradiction of advocating for environmental protections while funding the destruction of Gaza. The flyer for the event read: “Rep Katherine Clark voted to fund ecocide and genocide.” APD responded to the small protest with significant police presence, including a man who appeared to be an undercover officer, a K9 officer, and a drone. Early protest arrivals saw APD officers gathered around the drone in the Town Hall parking lot. While evidence points to coordination throughout the APD, K9 officer Michael Hogan responded on the scene that he had “no idea” who the drone belonged to when asked on camera. A second officer later confirmed, off-camera, that the drone belonged to APD. The undercover officer’s behavior, however, proved even more chilling. One attendee describes hearing the undercover officer calling her name, even though he was a stranger with no reason to know her name. It was really disconcerting when this random guy hiding out in the bushes behind me called me by my name. Later he started asking me questions. I think he was taking photos of us. [I wondered] Does APD have photos hanging around the station of community members? I looked on the APD website to try to confirm he was with them but they don’t publish names or photos, which seems odd for a department bragging about ‘community policing’. They can know who we are but we can’t know who they are?” Presumed undercover police officer, who called protesters by name from the bushes (Working Mass) The drone presence surprised many attendees. Some had not known about the APD drone prior to the protest, others reflected that they had not seen the drone used at larger protests that occurred after, such as No Kings or Free Her . Instead, it was seen only at the small pro-Palestine protest. Activists in Arlington describe a history of heightened involvement from APD regarding pro-Palestine activism. In 2024, Town Meeting members put forward a resolution (non-binding legislation showcasing town sentiments) supporting a permanent ceasefire in Gaza. During the discussion and vote, police officers were stationed inside of Town Hall — highly unusual for Town Meetings. It is unclear if APD made the decision to station officers or if a third party asked them to attend. K9 APD officer who denied knowing the drone belonged to the APD (Working Mass) Drone Acquired — No Town Meeting or Public Input Arlington Police Chief Juliann Flaherty confirmed over email that no public input process was conducted before acquiring the drone. The officer stated: We do not typically conduct public input processes for the acquisition of department equipment. While there is no formal review process, other police equipment budget requests have faced public scrutiny at Town Meetings. An amendment to remove $15,000 from the town budget passed in 2023 when APD requested that amount to purchase Bola Wraps , a compliance weapon that shoots kevlar ropes with barbed hooks around a person resisting police orders. Unlike the Bola Wraps, Town meeting members did not have an opportunity to discuss APD’s drone acquisition because the $6,000 drone was donated by the Rotary Club. Neither the drone nor the remote pilot training for officers appear in town budget documents from 2022 onward. Arlington Rotary Club did not respond to a request for comment. APD’s drone policy, which was provided by Chief Flaherty upon request, provides few guardrails on monitoring and recording people in public places. The privacy section states that without a warrant or other extenuating circumstances: [The operator] shall not intentionally record or transmit images of any location where a person would have a reasonable expectation of privacy. This leaves the use of drones to film protests and public events at the discretion of the police. There are no clear guidelines on when video can be recorded, only that the videos obtained “shall be handled in accordance with existing policy on data and records retention.” APD’s policy prohibits the use of the drone for “random surveillance activities,” but specifies a number of broad use cases that do not have clear definitions and can apply to most public gatherings. Examples of appropriate drone usage, according to APD policy, include “providing direction for crowd management and temporary perimeter security” and “photographic and video deployments.” This leaves room for APD to use drones to monitor and record protesters under the banner of crowd control and security. Police departments across the country have more access to footage, data, and technology to identify and track civilians than ever before. The country-wide network of Flock cameras and Automated Licence Plate Readers (ALPR) have been used by police departments to look up protest-related activity and associated vehicles without further justification for their searches. Further, Arlington police will soon be implementing body-worn cameras with the stated goal of increasing police accountability. That won’t be the only outcome. The other result will be recordings: many hours of footage, including protester and civilian interactions. Public Record Requests Show Zoomed-in Face Photographs Obtained through a Public Records Request, there is evidence obtained by Working Mass hat the drone captured zoomed in photos of several protesters’ faces on September 8, 2026. Records Clerk Suzanne Trunfio wrote that, additionally, “aerial images were captured to assess the surrounding area and perimeter for potential threats, including an individual positioned at an elevated location who could pose a danger to those below.” Three images provided are zoomed in to reveal faces, with a total of five individuals shown in the photos. None of the zoomed in photos show people in an “elevated location” as justified by Trunfio. The photos also show around six officers, not including the undercover officer, surrounding the small crowd of around thirty protesters from all sides. Aerial footage provided of the protest through public records request, showing no participant at any point of elevation, except police (Working Mass) Special Hostility Towards Protesters Since police responded to larger protests like No Kings with a fraction of the surveillance utilized for pro-Palestine demonstrations, questions arise about what types of protests are seen as a threat. Reporting by the Harvard Crimson shows that multiple city police departments collaborated with campus police to heavily monitor Pro-Palestine student protests after October 7, 2023, and this year, the city of Boston settled a police brutality lawsuit over the beating of protesters at a 2020 Black Lives Matters protest. The trade publication writings of former Arlington Police Lieutenant Richard Pedrini provide insight into how some police officers view different left-wing protest groups. Pedrini penned three articles in The Sentinel, a now defunct official publication of the Massachusetts Police Association, following the killing of a Weymouth police officer by a man undergoing a psychotic episode. He blamed criminal justice reform and progressive politicians for the death of the officer, stating: This animal needs to be put down, but unfortunately, this is Massachusetts. Besides describing a disabled man as an “animal,” Pedrini listed several protest movements and immigrants when expressing who he believes state politicians are siding with over police. “Drop the charade and get out on the streets with BLM, Antifa, and the ‘Resist’ crowd,” Pedrini wrote. “That’s all you’re good for. We know whose side you’re on and it’s not ours.” He continued working for APD until retiring in 2024, in spite of some town members calling for his removal. Throughout the process of requesting information from the Arlington Police Department, multiple employees stressed the need for community members to trust in the good intentions of their officers. Suzanne Trunfio included that “[APD] deployed the drone as a public safety measure to help protect everyone present… including those exercising their first amendment rights.” And Chief Flaherty wrote in a drone-focused email: While I understand the importance of asking questions and ensuring accountability, I also believe it is important to recognize the positive intentions and outcomes of these efforts rather than suggesting there are concerns where none have been identified. Of course, dismissing the press’s identification of residents’ concerns does not make those concerns disappear. While public-facing employees ask for community trust, a Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) audit of the department completed in 2020 reveals that officers feel animosity towards community members and police officers who speak out. The audit was initiated following public outcry over Lieutenant Pedrini’s violent rhetoric and sought to increase DEI within APD and their community interactions. Officer sentiments included that “community should not be involved in decisions regarding APD if they don’t know what police go through,” and referred to those who speak up as “extreme members of the public.” The report notes that the assessment had limitations because police culture can make it “harder/less safe for some members of the department to express criticism or concern about the actions of a fellow member.” This brings up questions around how likely APD is to hold itself accountable to already loose guidelines regarding the surveillance of protests and activists. At least one community member who attended the protest and preferred to stay anonymous said the drone policy leaves too much room for abuse. The APD Drone policy gives the police a broad spectrum of reasons to use the drones while it gives the people of Arlington very little safeguard against the encroachment and/or violation of their first amendment rights. The public has little to no understanding of these broad sweeping powers the police have in terms of surveillance and use of the photos and videos they collect through the drone. Avi R is a contributing writer to Working Mass. The post Arlington Police Used a Drone and Undercover Officer to Surveil and Photograph Pro-Palestine Protesters appeared first on Working Mass .

articles.title: Stella Lefty: Data Center Music
articles.author: Nikil Soto
articles.content: When Stella Lefty wrote the chorus to “Boston,” she was waiting in Nashville for a boy from outside Atlanta. Why Boston? She had a gig coming up there, she told Taste of Country . A month later she noticed it was also the name on the piano. Lefty posted the chorus on TikTok before there were verses to go with it. “Boston,” the breakout single from her debut album, Long Way Home , reached number two on the Billboard Hot 100 and number one on country radio. Try saying “I like it when you’re nice to me” aloud. Now hear how her bright, raspy voice tumbles into it over the acoustic guitar , pleased and a little embarrassed at what she’s admitted. Two verses would seem ample opportunity to give us one example of the guy being nice. Much of the case against Lefty rests on her birth certificate. Born Stella Lefkofsky, she grew up in Glencoe , on Chicago’s North Shore, went to Tulane University, and moved to Los Angeles. Her father, Eric Lefkofsky, cofounded Groupon and runs the health tech company Tempus AI. A billionaire’s daughter singing in a Southern accent about boys in pickup trucks was always going to take some grief. What’s worth resenting is how few of the people who build those pickups can afford to give their kids a few years to find out whether they’ve got a song in them. Give somebody an instrument and years to get good at it without having to earn a living, and now and then you get Gram Parsons . The grandson of a Florida citrus magnate, Parsons could sing about the riches he’d enjoyed and make you feel how badly he wanted to be up in a South Carolina oak tree again. Lefty put her own advantage nicely when she told Vanity Fair , “I didn’t have a stopwatch.” Country owes a great deal to people who worked by the clock for a wage. Southern millhands played some of its earliest dance music. Jimmie Rodgers learned from the black crews he worked alongside on the railroad. Even Trisha Yearwood’s gloriously juvenile “ She’s in Love With the Boy ” turns on what a boy can afford. Tommy proposes outside the Tastee-Freez with his high school ring. When Katie’s father objects, her mother reminds him what a catch he was as a penniless farm boy. By the last chorus, you’ve met four people and taken sides in a family fight. On Long Way Home , you can spend fourteen songs trying to get to know two people that well. In “ Whiskey ,” Lefty is so taken with the way a man talks that she’s struck dumb. We learn roughly as much about him as the bartender does — he likes his drinks on the rocks. I prefer “ Missing You ,” where she’s already nostalgic for the relationship while she’s still at his place wearing his T-shirt. He’s one door away. It’s funny and a little mortifying, which is how a person in love occasionally ought to sound. The plagiarism complaints are harder to shrug off. In “Boston,” you can hear the little hop in the melody of Noah Kahan’s “Stick Season,” right down to the way the singer comes back and does it again on the next line. It’s the only part of “Boston” you can hum to. Lefty told Vanity Fair she hadn’t been thinking about Kahan when she wrote it. She had, however, covered “Stick Season” on TikTok. Kahan got a writing credit after his team flagged the resemblance, shortly before the single came out. “Summer You Were Mine” deliberately borrows from the Chicks’ “There’s Your Trouble.” Rolling Stone verified that the interpolation was cleared before release. The original writers, Tia Sillers and Mark Selby, get their due. The tune fares worse. In the Chicks’ song , a woman has to explain to a lovesick man that the right girl is standing here talking to him. In Lefty’s song, what came between the lovers was September . Listeners heard Blake Shelton’s “ I’ll Name the Dogs ” in the album closer, “ Why Wouldn’t We .” Both choruses itemize what each partner brings to the relationship. Lefty has at least reassigned the job of telling the jokes. In October, after Lefty played an unreleased song called “Badly” at Nashville’s Bluebird Cafe, Shaylen and TAELA put it side by side with their own “WATCH THIS.” TAELA singled out the vocal phrasing and cadence. Allow for coincidence, unconscious imitation, and every last one of the credits, and you still have a debut filled with hooks from somebody else’s back catalog. That’s a poor return on fourteen chances to introduce yourself. There’s no need to believe in castigating people for their inherited privilege, but they should at least take advantage of all the time and security it affords. What explains Stella Lefty’s sudden rise, then? By August, the trade publication Hits was touting more than half a million videos using “Boston.” It had the feeling to many of an “op.” But the kids singing every word at CMA Fest settle the question of whether Lefty has real fans. Labels pay for clips that look like ordinary recommendations and have long helped manufacture demand for their artists. How much of that happened here, if any, remains an open question. You can forgive a listener a little skepticism the fifth time her phone invites her to discover a billionaire’s daughter. Lefty and her team tested takes on TikTok to see which songs to pursue, according to Crain’s Chicago Business . Once “Boston” took off, her label moved the album’s release from September to August . Here was a young woman with the means to take as much time as she liked, suddenly rushing to finish a record. Turns out somebody did have a stopwatch. Take “Something to Lose,” her duet with Vincent Mason. Their voices fit beautifully together. On the record, they meet at 2 in the morning in “a Southern state.” In life, they met at Schulman’s in East Nashville. She brought three friends as chaperones. Her producer remembers drinking Chartreuse. Her cowriter Grace Enger got a burger inside while Lefty and Mason flirted outside. All those songwriters at the bar, and somehow the burger and the Chartreuse didn’t make the cut. For all I know, the person who poured that Chartreuse has a worse country record in them than Stella Lefty. I’d happily run the risk of hearing it. A billionaire’s daughter gets the time off first and a chance to find out how good she is. The results turned out to be derivative and mediocre. articles.title: TrumpCare
articles.author: Paul deLespinasse
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Now that Democrats will control both house of Congress, one naturally wonders whether they can work with President Trump. A hopeful sign has come from the new senator from Michigan. Abdul El-Sayed wants to enact Medicare For All. He recently suggested that it be called TrumpCare ! Since the president loves to have things named for himself, this is a brilliant idea. Getting Trump’s support would greatly improve insurance reform’s chances of getting through Congress. Most Republicans would have to fall in line. Don’t consider this idea impossible. After all, it was the militant anti-Communist Richard Nixon who ended America’s total hostility to Communist China. And President Trump himself has indicated possible interest in the idea, since he reposted El-Sayed’s mockup of a TrumpCare gold card on his social media site. Related: Impeachment Could Become A Powerful Tool, But Probably Not Against A President The idea of enlisting Trump to enact Medicare For All is not a new one. During his first administration the New York Times reported that his friend Christopher Ruddy—founder and CEO of conservative NewsMax—was urging him to support a single-payer insurance system to replace Obamacare. This did not amaze me. Single-payer would promote conservative values like efficiency and simplicity. And it would eliminate separate governmental insurance programs for veterans, children, native Americans, and the poor. Strong presidential leadership could help overcome the chief political obstacle to insurance reform—how it would be financed. Strong leadership is essential here. Reform supporters grossly underestimate how much income taxes must be increased. Medical care, now about one fifth of GDP, cannot be financed by a small tax increase. Opponents—including powerful vested medical and insurance interests—take advantage of a general misunderstanding of how much people are already paying for insurance. They claim the program would leave less money in people’s pockets, which is not true. Most American families get insurance through their jobs and are unaware that as workers they are paying for all of its very high cost. They only see what they pay directly , the “employees’ share” plus their own deductibles and co-pays. They don’t realize that they are also paying the so-called “employers share”, the major portion of their insurance costs, indirectly in the form of lower wages. Employers pay for workers’ insurance out of the same pot from which they pay wages and salaries. What they remit for insurance is not available for wages. Americans will be comparing an obvious tax increase with what looks like a much smaller expense in the present system. Related: One Sided View of Preposterous Lawsuit At PBS But the new system will actually be cheaper because the current system is horribly inefficient. It features many different insurance companies and insurance policies, each with its own coverage, exclusions, and “in-network” doctors and hospitals. Coping with this complexity costs the average doctor around $80,000-$100,000 per year for clerical assistance, costs that must be paid for by patients or their self-financed insurance. And the insurance companies have considerable administrative expenses, dividends, and high executive salaries. A single-payer system, eliminating billing complexity and private profits, would greatly reduce the total cost of medical care. The large tax increase needed to support insurance would therefore cost the average worker less than he or she is already paying, directly and indirectly. Employers, no longer remitting large amounts to insure their workers, should be required to pass those savings along as wage increases. This would both be fair and make selling the program to the public easier. Selling the program to the public is where Donald Trump—skilled at getting public attention and selling his ideas—could come in. It might take someone like him to convince people that single-payer insurance would leave them, on average, with a bit more cash in their pockets. In an era when AI may be destroying jobs, single-payer’s decoupling of insurance from employment would also relieve a great deal of anxiety. Democrats, despite reservations about Trump, should take advantage of his skills to advance their policy priorities if he is interested in co-operating. Related: A Major Political Question: To Whom Did God Give Land? One caveat though: Let’s not assume that the new program should just be an expansion of Medicare to everyone. The president should appoint a task force of experts to study the strengths and weaknesses of foreign medical insurance systems. The task force should report its findings and recommendations within one year, so that Congress could enact a program covering everyone before Mr. Trump’s term expires. Any activity comprising a fifth of the GDP cannot be turned on a dime. The transition from the current insurance system would need to be carefully planned to make it as graceful and easy on everybody as possible. Go for it, Senator-elect El-Sayed! Go for it, President Trump! Let’s hear it for TrumpCare!

articles.title: Effective Altruism Is Increasingly Just Funding Itself
articles.author: Jacob Davis
articles.content: The basic pitch for effective altruism (EA) is simple: charitable giving is an investment, whose return is in others’ well-being rather than your financial betterment. Given that it’s an investment, it makes sense to look for a strong, measurable return from wherever you choose to donate. After all, if you really care about others being well-off, you should be at least as conscientious about these investments as you are about your retirement savings. This is, to say the least, a controversial approach to charity. It has many detractors: those who argue that the approach flattens value to numbers in a spreadsheet, or that it ignores the place of solidarity and political organizing. But the ethic also has its undeniable appeal. Among effective altruists, the standard example of effective giving is usually the Against Malaria Foundation (AMF), which distributes insecticide-laced bed nets in sub-Saharan Africa to combat mosquito-borne illness. It is hard to argue that AMF is not a better place to give your money than many competing organizations, like various sketchy “ voluntourism ” outfits or microloan creditors . Where many critiques of EA miss the mark is in taking this pitch at face value. In reality, as measured by volume of money flow, EA is more a means of cultivating a self-selecting, insular subculture based around the tech industry. The biggest objection that can be laid against it is not that its founding principles are misguided, but that they have come to play third or fourth fiddle to building a playground and safety net for a small, privileged portion of the global population. Short-Term vs. Long-Term EA Within EA, a distinction is sometimes drawn between “long-term” and “short-term” effective altruism. Classic poster children like AMF almost all fall on the “short-term” side of the split: concrete, clearly specifiable interventions to promote measurable goods in the present or near future. “Long-term” cause areas are generally more nebulous or speculative: preparations for future pandemics, the eventual curtailment of wild animal suffering, or (above all) artificial intelligence safety. Long-term cause areas generally, and AI safety specifically, have come to dominate EA organizing. One measure of this is the recent spending decisions of Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy), the dominant EA grant-making body. In 2025 , nearly $490 million of Coefficient Giving’s roughly $840 million in grants were dedicated to “long-term and existential risk,” overwhelmingly in AI safety. This is in contrast to the approximately $150 million spent on global health and development, the classic “short-term” general cause area. This spending strategy is puzzling, under traditional EA principles. As Coefficient Giving states on its funding page, effective altruists deliberately focus on funding for problems that are important , neglected , and tractable . Without prejudice to the issue’s importance, there is a growing consensus among concerned parties that AI safety is not currently tractable: there is widespread recognition that no robust technical road map to safe AI has been, or will likely soon be, forthcoming. And leading AI safety organization Anthropic just opened its initial public offering (IPO) at around $1.5 trillion — prompting disillusionment even within EA. Rarely in human history has any problem been less economically neglected. Anthropic, like OpenAI before it, highlights the double-edged nature of much technical AI safety research. In the eyes of most effective altruists, developing AI capabilities is directly opposed to the goal of AI safety. And yet most avenues of technical safety research go hand-in-hand with capabilities development; indeed, this is a criticism lobbed against AI safety initiatives by many effective altruists. Research projects on interpretability , reinforcement learning with human feedback, and thinking traces have all failed to realize the elusive dream of AI “alignment” but have provided considerable returns to sheer performance levels. What AI safety funding does offer is an opportunity to spread money around a self-selecting community of EA researchers and activists. A dizzying number of conferences, think tanks, and fellowships have sprung up to study the topic, backed by funders like Coefficient Giving. Much as a liberal-interventionist foreign policy makes for “ a full-employment strategy for the foreign policy establishment,” so the focus on AI safety provides the AI safety community abundant opportunity for remunerative work and stimulating play. Effective Altruism for Profit Perhaps no organization better illustrates these tendencies than Manifund , a San Francisco–based fundraising body closely tied to the EA community. Whereas Coefficient Giving has historically acted mainly as a channel for the philanthropy of billionaire couple Dustin Moskovitz and Cari Tuna, Manifund is designed to invite funding from a range of interested onlookers. Much of this fundraising is conducted through Manifund’s “impact certificate ecosystem,” which they describe as “ like Kickstarter meets the stock market .” The organization also subscribes to a principle of full transparency, making its grant-making process unusually accessible. Many of its grant choices are atypical, to say the least. In a recent blog post, for example, Manifund CEO and cofounder Austin Chen explains a number of routes the organization uses to funnel donor money into for-profit ventures — in spite of Manifund’s status as a 501(c)3 tax-exempt non-profit. These range from the relatively innocuous (commissions for specific services) to the legal but abnormal (outright investment). Manifund has adopted more indirect means of supporting for-profit entities, as well. For example, it is responsible for funding and running Mox , an EA workspace and community hub in Downtown San Francisco. In addition to offering work space for individual paying members, Mox — which shares Chen as head — plays host to several EA-affiliated small businesses. And this summer, Mox and Manifund co-organized Surplus , a software start-up incubator offering generous seed funding and pitch opportunities to successful applicants. Similarly unorthodox have been the charity’s recent hiring decisions. Against considerable uproar, Manifund recently hired effective altruist and convicted fraudster Caroline Ellison to serve on its administrative staff. In 2024, Ellison was sentenced to two years’ incarceration in connection with her roles at cryptocurrency trading firm Alameda Research and sister company FTX. She has since July played a major role alongside Chen in approving and directing grant decisions at Manifund, as well as contributing to the charity’s Substack. This decision prompted considerable backlash from the EA community. Complaints stemmed partly from concerns about optics, given the extremely negative attention Ellison had already attracted to EA. But there were also more direct concerns about her trustworthiness and competence, especially in a financially responsible role, as well as resentment from victims of fraud connected to FTX and Alameda Research. Chen defended the decision in the September blog post announcing the hire, offering among other reasons a sense of indebtedness to FTX: I felt a keen debt to the FTX Future Fund. They provided seed funding for Manifold. They funded the retreat which drew me into the EA community, and the conference where I met my wife. Much of Manifund’s work today is directly inspired by the Future Fund’s approach . The Future Fund was the philanthropic wing of FTX, which at the time was linked to fraudulently acquired funds siphoned from the exchange’s account holders. In addition to Manifund, the Future Fund supported a number of EA-related causes, primarily related to AI safety and pandemic prevention. The Transfer of Wealth In all of these capacities, Manifund has consistently deprioritized “short-term” EA work of the sort exemplified by AMF. Often, this has been in favour of recognizable “long-term” cause areas, like AI safety. But sometimes its beneficiaries have not even clearly fit this more extensive mold and instead have been connected to EA more through cultural and ideological affinity. An easy indication of this is the official breakdown of Manifund grants by cause area. Best-funded is “ Technical AI Safety ” at over $8 million, coming out ahead of similarly AI-dominated causes like “ AI Governance ” ($5.2 million) and “ Global Catastrophic Risks ” ($4.7 million). All of these come out ahead of “ Global Health and Development ,” which clocks in at a comparatively meagre $436,000. (Cause areas are not mutually exclusive, so some of these funding amounts overlap.) The immediate net effect of this outsize investment in technical AI safety is a transfer of wealth to the EA-dominated AI safety research community. Existing technical AI safety initiatives are effectively all research- or education-oriented: given the lack of any widely recognized way of implementing AI safety, the main place for funding to go is to researchers either currently trying to develop strategies for AI safety or learning what is needed to do the same. EA-affiliated AI governance initiatives, in turn, are carried out in close coordination with technical researchers and draw from a similar subcultural pool. Many non-AI projects with heavy support from Manifund similarly circulate the EA cash pool among other effective altruists. For example, Manifund has raised $132,000 in funding for “ human intelligence amplification @ Berkeley Genomics Project” — an attempt to breed a new generation of hyperintelligent humans through genomic engineering, in the hopes that they may be better suited to design safe AI systems. Setting aside any ethical considerations, the project is unlikely to generate immediate fruit. Rather, the main immediate impact is the opportunity to conduct highly speculative bioengineering research much in vogue among effective altruists. The same tendency is even more directly on display in the “ EA Community ” category ($1.6 million). Best-funded of all projects in the category, after Mox, is Lightcone Infrastructure — the common funding and governing body of LessWrong and the EA hotel turned event venue Lighthaven. Lighthaven, acquired by Lightcone in 2022 ( reportedly with the substantial financial assistance of FTX), has subsequently hosted a number of conferences, programs, and parties associated with the EA community in the Bay Area. More indirect support from Manifund, such as through Mox, continues this trend. Some of the start-ups using Mox’s office space, for example, are only very dubiously philanthropic ventures. They include The Relationship Company (a dating app “making AI systems that understand who you are and find people you’d genuinely connect with”) and Stardrift (an AI-based travel agency). Expanding the Circle A common metaphor used to explain EA to outsiders is the “ circle of concern .” Moral progress, in this story, is largely a matter of expanding this “circle:” the range of people, animals, and things about which one cares. At the center of your circle is you, whom you will care about even if you are maximally greedy and selfish. Beyond that lie family, neighbors, countrymen, humanity writ large, and the animal kingdom, at ever wider removes. Effective altruism, at its best, is about maintaining a wide circle of concern, in a self-consciously rational way. The irony in this tale is that EA has often had the opposite effect. Where charitable donations might otherwise have gone to distant victims of poverty, illness, and disaster, many EA organizations have instead channeled them primarily to one another. Rather than expanding its devotees’ circle of concern, effective altruism has come to consist largely in narrowing that circle to effective altruists.
