articles.title: AIPAC Get What It Paid For
articles.author: William J. Astore
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. I made the mistake of going on X/Twitter this morning, where I came across Hakeem Jeffries saying he and the Democrats are going to address the affordability crisis in America. Is he going to do that by raising the federal minimum wage to $20 an hour? Of course not. He provided no specifics. Here’s an excerpt from a recent interview of Jeffries: So from our standpoint, we want to do things like end this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has made life way too expensive. We need to stop the Trump Tariffs. We need to reverse the Medicaid cuts that put the health insurance of millions of Americans at risk and threatens to close hospitals all over the place. We certainly need to reverse the SNAP cuts. And we need to extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits. OK, so he wants to end the Iran war, but he doesn’t say how. I’ve seen where he’s against cutting Congressional funding for that war, which would be the quickest way to end it. He’s against impeaching President Trump for starting “this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran.” So what, exactly, is Jeffries going to do except bloviate? Furthermore, we know he’s on the AIPAC payroll big time, and Zionist Israel wants this war, so chances are Jeffries will do nothing more than blather on. Related: Is the Media Selling Another War? The Iran Dirty Bomb Allegations There’s no vision, no action, coming from Jeffries. At best, he wants to return to the Biden years, tinkering around the edges, supporting policies that are attractive to health insurance companies, big pharma, the status quo. Is that what the “Blunami” was all about? Incremental change to return us (if we’re lucky) to 2022? Jeffries opposes Medicare for All or any other single-payer government health care system. He refuses to support raising the minimum wage to $20 an hour. (He says it should be raised but provides no figure, so maybe he thinks $7.50 might be a decent hourly rate.) He won’t oppose weapons sales to Israel and he’ll never say Israel is engaged in a genocide in Gaza. Nor will he call for major cuts to Pentagon spending. Jeffries is Obama 2.0 without the oratorical skills and charisma. Just as Obama discarded his followers and a progressive agenda after his dramatic victory in 2008—wait a moment, I take that back. Obama was never really for “change” in the way that his followers believed him to be. As Congressman Dennis Kucinich said about Obama, “check his scorecard” in the Senate, where Obama was basically a neoliberal Clintonist. When President Obama bailed out the banks and rewarded the bankers while screwing American workers and homeowners, that was eminently predictable based on his scorecard and the fact that Wall Street had embraced him and funded his campaign. Check Hakeem Jeffries’ scorecard and who funds him and it’s obvious he’s going to betray American workers. And the danger is what these workers reach for in 2028 when they turn away from his empty and exploitative phoniness. They are likely to turn toward a populist Republican promising a form of vengeance through retrograde policies. As I looked at that image of Jeffries, the song “Smiling Faces” popped into my head. Some choice lyrics: Smiling faces, smiling faces, sometimes They don’t tell the truth Smiling faces, smiling faces tell lies and I got proof Oh, oh, yeah Can you blame workers for wanting some form of vengeance, no matter how wrongheaded or counterproductive, when they’ve been betrayed so often by liars like Jeffries? What a great song!

articles.title: Will Democrats Choose Peace
articles.author: Medea Benjamin, Nicolas Davies
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. As Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January, they face a critical choice on Ukraine: Will they help bring an end to a devastating war that is killing and wounding hundreds of thousands of people, or will they double down on a failed strategy of sending more weapons, pouring billions more dollars into the war, and rejecting opportunities for diplomacy? While Trump has renewed efforts to seek a negotiated solution to the war, which he had promised to solve on the first day of his second term, Democrats in Congress appear ready to reject diplomacy and increase support for the war. The likely incoming House committee chairs Gregory Meeks (Foreign Affairs), Adam Smith (Armed Services) and Jim Himes (Intelligence) have pledged legislation to compel Trump to provide greater military, economic and intelligence support to Ukraine. Democrats are reportedly considering a new Ukraine aid package of up to $15 billion, even as Trump has requested no new Ukraine funding in his 2027 military budget. The effort has bipartisan backing, with Republicans such as Rep. Joe Wilson and Sen. Roger Wicker pushing for continued military aid and tougher sanctions on Russia. Congress could also seek to reverse Trump's easing of sanctions, setting up a confrontation over whether Washington should increase pressure on Russia or prioritize a negotiated settlement. Meanwhile, a new series of talks between the U.S., Russia and Ukraine began in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11. As in previous talks, they agreed on another prisoner exchange, but there was no breakthrough on ending the war. Related: 10 Reasons Hakeem Jeffries Should Not Be Speaker of the House As Ukraine suffers mounting loss of life, widespread destruction and economic devastation, Russia bears full responsibility for launching its illegal invasion and continuing its brutal attacks. NATO leaders, whose military officers shape and support Ukraine’s war strategy from their joint headquarters at the Wiesbaden US air base in Germany, blame the ongoing conflict solely on Russia, relying on a thick fog of propaganda to evade accountability for their own roles in Ukraine’s destruction. When the Democrats take charge in Congress, they will find that neither President Zelenskyy nor his European allies have budged from the no-negotiations policy that the Biden administration and then British prime minister Boris Johnson pressured Ukraine and NATO into adopting in April 2022. After only six weeks of war, Johnson marched into Kyiv and told Zelenskyy to stop negotiating with Putin and commit to a long war, with the ill-defined goal of “weakening” Russia. Johnson persuaded Zelenskyy to abandon peace talks in Istanbul, where Russia had already agreed to the broad terms of a Ukrainian peace proposal. Falsely claiming to speak for the “ collective West ,” Johnson refused to back any agreement with Russia, and promised Zelenskyy that the UK was “in it for the long run.” Four and a half years later, some responsible party in the western world must fess up to the reality that this policy has failed miserably, militarizing and strengthening Russia instead of weakening it. Then they must take a fresh, unbiased look at where the war stands and what can be done to end it, if they are to save the Ukrainian people from the catastrophe of a brutal war of attrition fought to the bitter end. It is one thing to condemn Russia for launching a devastating war; it is quite another to prolong that war in an effort to punish Russia, at the cost of countless Ukrainian lives. According to an October Rating Group poll reported by the Ukrainian news agency UNN, more than 80% of Ukrainians now support a negotiated peace with Russia, while 56% say they would agree to territorial concessions if they are linked to security guarantees. Only 21% now support an unlimited war to try to restore Ukraine’s pre-2014 borders. Related: Books or Bombs? French Students Protest Education Cuts as Military Spending Rises Former UN Assistant Secretary General Michael von der Schulenburg, now a European Member of Parliament from Germany, is warning that Ukraine is close to collapse, and that the US and Europe’s refusal to face that reality risks making the final stages of the war even more disastrous. While Ukraine has inflicted serious damage inside Russia, including destroying a major section of the Kerch Strait bridge between Russia and Crimea, Russia has intensified its attacks on bridges across the Dnipro River, which could effectively cut Ukraine in half. Russia is methodically destroying Ukraine’s energy and transport infrastructure, and has closed the port of Odesa, the main outlet for Ukraine’s exports. If Ukraine should permanently lose Odesa, it would be left with no port on the Black Sea for its main exports of grains and cooking oil. War casualties, mass flight from the country and territorial losses have already reduced Ukraine’s population from 52 million in 1992 to probably less than half that today. A violent, climactic end to the war would trigger a new exodus. Instead of millions of women and children returning to rebuild their shattered country, young men whom martial law has prevented from leaving will finally leave to join family members in their new lives abroad. European officials also held talks with the US and Ukraine on November 10th, but without Russia, before meeting again with President Zelenskyy at a European summit in Dublin. Kaja Kallas, the EU’s unelected High Representative for Foreign Policy, declared the new negotiations dead-on-arrival, telling Reuters, “So far they have just been pretending that they negotiate because we haven’t seen any ⁠goodwill from the Russian side.” Kallas hasn’t shown any goodwill either, and is still clinging to Biden and Johnson’s playbook, preemptively rejecting any chance for diplomacy. Related: The Urgency of Recognizing the Ansar Allah Government in Yemen But some of Europe’s elected leaders are rightly wary of Kallas’s virulent Russophobia and militarism, and have refused to appoint her as the sole EU representative to the new round of talks. Many of their populations are in open revolt against huge increases in military spending, since NATO agreed to Trump’s demand that each NATO country should spend 5% of GDP on its military, although many of them had not even met its previous 2% target. Only the socialist government of Pedro Sanchez in Spain has explicitly rejected any increase in military spending for Trump’s new arms race in Europe. Meanwhile, on November 18, the European Commission proposed a new $49 billion aid package for Ukraine for 2027 - $27 billion in military aid and $22 billion in budgetary support. But Bulgaria, Hungary, Czechia and Slovakia have already announced that they won’t contribute, and Poland has ruled out further contributions to a separate NATO program that buys weapons for Ukraine. As the public in Europe take to the streets demanding that their taxes be spent on healthcare, housing and education , not on weapons and war, their leaders smugly claim that they are funding, and in some cases participating actively in the war in Ukraine to enforce the UN Charter and international law. US allies watch mostly in silence as the United States routinely violates Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, which prohibits the threat or use of force against other countries. Yet they treat Russia’s violation of the same article against Ukraine as justification for an endless, bloody war, sacrificing a generation of Ukrainians, but not their own young people. But the UN Charter’s Article 2(4) is not a blank check for endless war. Quite the opposite. US and European leaders must also comply with Article 2(3), which commits all countries to resolving their disputes peacefully, and Article 33, which spells out that obligation in more detail. This commitment to the “pacific resolution of disputes” is the basis for the prohibition on the threat or use of force. Nowhere does the Charter say that Articles 2(3) and 33 cease to apply once another country has violated Article 2(4). To interpret the Charter that way would be a recipe for endless war, which is precisely what the West’s deliberate misinterpretation of the Charter has led to in Ukraine. Related: Stop the War Machine: Start Rebuilding America Russia’s guilt for its aggression against Ukraine does not absolve Western leaders for their own violations of the UN Charter. Illegally rejecting negotiations and diplomacy in favor of prolonging a war Ukraine cannot win militarily, they have sacrificed Ukraine and its brave people on the altar of their geopolitical ambitions, as they have done to countless other countries. But there is also a political price to pay for perpetuating endless wars. Even Trump and Vance have admitted that their illegal war on Iran lost the election for the Republicans, and Americans did not vote to end one illegal war in order to escalate another. Those who are old enough to remember 2008 can recall how Barack Obama was hailed as a peace candidate because he promised to end the US war in Iraq, but then escalated the US war in Afghanistan, prolonging it for another 13 years. Did Obama’s party learn nothing from that experience? Will the Democrats now make a similar miscalculation in Ukraine? Or will they listen to voices urging peace and diplomacy, like the war-wise veterans in the Eisenhower Media Network and Veterans for Peace ? A post-election Reuters/Ipsos poll published on November 10th shows that US voters have connected the dots between the war on Iran and their own economic problems. They want their government to reorient its priorities from wars overseas, support for Israel and record military spending to the neglected needs of working Americans. Most of the American public now see through the false narratives that support corrupt oligarchic policies, from billionaire tax breaks to genocide in Palestine and war on Iran. The Ukraine war has faded from the headlines, but a Democratic effort to provide more war funding or escalate the war could bring it back into the spotlight, prompting millions of Americans to ask the same hard questions about Ukraine that they have been asking about Israel and Iran. Here are a few such questions, and some sources that can help to answer them. Related: Lula, Trump and Bolsonaro: Why Brazil’s 2026 Election Matters to the World How did NATO expansion betray US commitments to Russia, revive the Cold War and lead to war in Ukraine, as veteran US diplomats warned that it would? See prescient warnings by George Kennan , the Arms Control Association and Ambassador to Moscow (later CIA Director) William Burns . How did the violent overthrow of Ukraine’s elected Yanukovich government in 2014 lead to the disintegration of Ukraine? See a June 2014 Gallup poll in which only about 50% of the population of Ukraine recognized the new government as legitimate , and the deadly violence of the Right Sector militia and right-wing Svoboda party against Ukrainians who rejected the US-backed regime change. How did the 2015 Minsk II Accord succeed in deescalating the post-coup civil war, but fail to resolve Ukraine’s political divisions ? See this interview with former OSCE ceasefire monitor Benoît Paré, who explains that pro-Ukrainian government forces were responsible for nearly three-quarters of the civilian casualties in Donbas between 2016 and 2018, as Ukraine shifted from granting autonomy to Donbas, which it agreed to in Minsk, to planning to take it back by force, with NATO support, weapons and training . What was the Istanbul agreement of March 2022, and why did Ukrainian negotiators celebrate its success but then abandon it at the insistence of the US and UK? The then Israeli prime minister Naftali Bennett and former German Chancellor Gerhard Schroder were both involved in those negotiations, and have given consistent accounts of the US role in blocking them. And what of the West’s endless claims that Russia is always just on the verge of defeat in Ukraine, despite President Zelenskyy warning that Russia has ten times the artillery and 30 times the airpower of Ukraine? Can we believe Ukrainian and Western claims that Russia is suffering more casualties than Ukraine, despite this huge imbalance in the explosive weapons that cause the most casualties: bombs, missiles, drones and artillery shells? See this interview with Alexander Grable, a researcher in the Department of War Studies at King’s College, London. Related: Why America’s Trillion-Dollar War Machine Is Failing in Iran Despite the dense fog of propaganda from all sides, it is clear that Ukraine cannot defeat Russia, which means it will not militarily recover all the territory it has lost since 2014. In any case, large majorities in Crimea , Luhansk and Donetsk already voted to secede from Ukraine. But a peace agreement could include internationally recognized referenda in those areas, maybe even with a choice between autonomy within Ukraine (as in the Minsk Accords) and international recognition as provinces of Russia. Russia has occupied more territory since the US and UK undermined the Istanbul agreement in 2022. But that lost chance for peace shows that agreement is possible. The longer this war goes on, the greater the scale of death and destruction will be, and the more precarious the future that Ukraine will face when it finally ends. The new Democratic leaders in Congress will have a chance to “seize the moment,” as General Mark Milley, then the Chairman of the US Joint Chiefs of Staff, implored Biden and Zelenskyy to do in November 2022, after a successful Ukrainian counteroffensive led to a Russian withdrawal from the city of Kherson. Tragically, General Milley was ignored. If the Democrats want to seize this new moment to make peace, General Milley, now a Distinguished Fellow at Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service, would be a more serious choice as a US negotiator than Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, who are real estate developers, not diplomats. Neither Trump and his real estate brokers nor Europe’s unpopular leaders can act as impartial mediators, since their countries are all parties to the war. We would much prefer to see the UN and the OSCE (Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe) step in to conduct legitimate multilateral diplomacy rooted in international law, as they have done in other conflicts, and also to monitor any ceasefire, as the OSCE did in Donbas from 2015 to 2022. But it is ultimately Russia and Ukraine that must make peace, regardless of who plays the role of mediator. The most important role the United States and its European allies can play is to support that process, not undermine it, as they did in April 2022, as European leaders are still doing, and as the Democrats in Congress risk doing too, if they try to resurrect Biden’s failed playbook. It’s a measure of the futility of this war that the peace plan the US and UK torpedoed in April 2022 still offers a basic model for what both sides may be willing to accept in a new peace agreement. The essence of the plan was simply to agree that Ukraine will not join NATO and will be a neutral country, like Austria during the “old” Cold War; not a battleground between East and West, but a bridge between them that can reap the benefits of trade and political and cultural connections with both. But first, Ukraine must have peace, and we urge the new Democratic majority in Congress to seize the moment.

articles.title: The Battle Over BAAJA and “Permitting Reform” Reinforces the Necessity of Expropriating Capital for Planetary Survival — The Black Alliance for Peace
articles.content: “If one were forced for the sake of clarity to define [fascism] in a word, that word would be ‘reform.’” - George Jackson November 23, 2026 – Less than three weeks after the ‘Blue Wave,’ celebrated by the Democratic Party and its allies, U.S. Senate and House Democrats seem poised to join their Republican colleagues to advance the fascist, neoliberal march by passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). The bill sailed through the Senate with a significant number of Democrats, including current Minority Leader Schumer, joining the Republicans to secure its passage. The bill now moves to the House, where Republicans are working to fast-track it to President Trump’s desk for signature. Specifically, the bill makes major changes to environmental laws like the Clean Water Act and National Environmental Policy Act to speed up the development of energy projects. If enacted, it will erode environmental protections, land use regulations, and tribal sovereignty in a way that will devastate Black, Indigenous, and working-class communities, as well as the ecosystems they inhabit, under the guise of “permitting reform”. The Black Alliance for Peace denounces both the substance of the bill and the Democratic Party’s repudiation of the midterm elections’ popular rejection of the neoliberal status quo. Both aspects represent acts of economic, class, and environmental warfare against the working class; Black, Indigenous, and all oppressed peoples throughout the United States; and the planet. This bill – this “reform” – is not merely a question of environmental protections, but is rooted in domestic and global (neo)colonial usurpation of Indigenous sovereignty and the collective self-determination of the masses within the United States to achieve their People(s)-Centered Human Rights . It will further open the door for capitalist predation of oppressed and colonized peoples and communities throughout the United States, while reducing the already paltry legal avenues available to frontline communities and grassroots movements to oppose the destruction and poisoning of their lands, waters, and air. This comes at a time when the U.S. government and major technology companies are determined to continue the hyperscale data center buildout that is disproportionately being targeted at Black and Brown communities with little public input , and has already been accompanied by severe environmental deregulation in the past year . The battle against this specific bill has not been without resistance, particularly from Indigenous movements and communities over the attacks against tribal sovereignty and illegal land seizures that this bill would allow, as well as from movements against hyperscale data centers from across the country. However, what this bill and the battle around it reveal is that as long as the struggle for climate and environmental liberation is confined to legal determinations and fights against individual corporate or state projects, the masses are bound to lose. There can be no “just transition” or planetary survival with human dignity without the expropriation of capital, and continuing to live under the illusion that this class struggle can be avoided will only allow for the continued destabilization, disabling, and poisoning of our people and ecosystems. As BAP wrote this past April after the First Conference for Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels, “We maintain it is those peoples, nations, communities who paid the price that must define the solutions for a fossil-free future – against the greenwashing and liberal reformist tendencies that too often structure and dominate these conversations. There can be no climate and environmental justice without climate and environmental liberation, and there can be no path toward liberation that is not dedicated to fighting the interlocking systems of oppression that still shackle our people: imperialism, capitalism, (neo)colonialism, patriarchy, militarism, and white supremacy. This requires political clarity, concrete action, and sustained struggle…It is clear to BAP that while we must engage the institutions of power and decision-making ability, the only path forward from fossil fuel dependency and economy is the defeat of those interlocking systems of oppression through a unified, protracted struggle and social revolution based in People(s)-Centered Human Rights.” This task remains the same, and the necessity of coordinated anti-imperialist struggle against the capitalist system and the domination of fossil fuel and tech oligopoly, as well as the neocolonial political officials that serve them, is only more urgent. No Compromise, No Retreat.

articles.title: New Deal Majority
articles.author: John Peeler
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Since the Civil War, scholars have found a persistent pattern in party competition in this country. One party tends to win the majority of votes nationally for several consecutive elections. Then some critical event such as a depression leads a critical mass of voters to switch loyalties. The former minority party becomes the normal majority. After the Civil War, the Republicans were the normal majority, narrowly until 1896, then overwhelmingly until the Great Depression. The shock of the Depression and the vigor of the New Deal response then established the Democrats as the normal majority until the late 1960s. The Civil Rights movement, the unpopular Vietnam War, and widespread protests eroded the Democratic hegemony, allowing the narrow election of Richard Nixon in 1968. The 1970s were a transitional period marked by the Watergate scandal and the resignation of President Nixon. An era of Republican dominance emerged with Ronald Reagan’s election in 1980, but lasted only until George H.W. Bush’s defeat by Bill Clinton in 1992. Related: When Democracy Strikes Back: Trump, Orbán, and Pinochet Since 1992, there has been no nationally dominant party. Clinton lost his congressional majority in 1994, but was easily reelected in 1996. In 2000, voters were almost evenly divided in an election decided by the Supreme Court in Bush v. Gore . Bush and Obama were each reelected, but then saw their opposition capture the presidency. Trump and Biden were each denied reelection, and probably the Republican successor to Trump will lose to the Democrat in 2028. A key feature of the earlier periods of party hegemony was that most voters identified with either the Republicans or the Democrats. Independent voters were relatively few. Now, however, in this era of no party hegemony, the weight of independents has increased. By definition, independents are not attached to either party (though many may lean toward one or the other). In this year’s election, independents determined outcomes in contest after contest. The Democrats could not have achieved their strong majorities without independent voters. The Democrats now have a strategic choice. They can accept the logic of the current no-hegemony era, and just play for the victory in 2028. That would entail highlighting the misdeeds and unpopularity of Trump and his party, and pursuing policies to undo the many evils that Trump has perpetrated. That’s the line of least resistance. But that’s a virtual guarantee that the Democratic president elected in 2028 will be defeated in 2032. And most likely, s/he will lose the congressional majorities in the midterms of 2030. The reason lies in a fundamental reality of American life over the last fifty years. Our society has grown steadily more economically unequal. Today average people can barely make ends meet with two full-time workers. People are more and more indebted. They are less likely to afford to buy a home. As successive elected governments in this century have failed to address this economic reality, they have been turned out of office: Bush II, Obama, Trump I, Biden, and (probably) Trump II’s successor. Related: Trump's Political Collapse Was Entirely His Own Making The second choice the Democrats have is to undertake to rectify this half-century injustice, to take concrete steps rapidly improving the well-being and security of most people. That will include reversing the tax cuts for the wealthy that Republicans since Reagan have enacted. Medicare for All would be a key accomplishment, but minimally, Obamacare and Medicaid should have the Trump cuts reversed. Social Security should be put on a stable basis. These are just some of the major reforms that should be undertaken to make life better for most people. If the Democrats pursue this second course, they will have the chance to establish a new period of Democratic hegemony like that which started with the New Deal. The Republicans, meanwhile, must choose between being a right-wing MAGA minority party, and, on the other hand, contesting the independents they lost in this year’s election. If they choose the latter, that would be good for our democracy: for democracy to work in the long term, it needs at least two parties competing, both committed to democracy. Now, sadly, only one party is committed to democracy.

articles.title: The 1956 Hungarian Counterrevolution and Jacobin’s False Narrative of a “Working-class Revolt”
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By Nikos Mottas November 11, 2026 In Defense of Communism Seventy years after the counterrevolutionary events of 1956, Hungary remains a powerful reminder that the struggle between socialism and capitalism does not end with the overthrow of bourgeois power. The restoration of capitalism was not an abstract possibility, nor was the danger of counterrevolution confined to external imperialist intervention. It could also emerge through the exploitation of internal contradictions, political mistakes and the advance of opportunism within the communist movement itself. The events of October–November 1956 demonstrated how genuine popular grievances could become intertwined with the activities of reactionary forces seeking to overthrow socialist power. They also exposed the dangers created when ideological confusion and political weaknesses allowed imperialism to exploit a crisis that had developed within socialist society. Yet seven decades later, the social-democratic magazine Jacobin presents a seemingly radical interpretation of 1956 that nevertheless echoes a central premise of dominant bourgeois historiography. In a recent article, Adam Fabry and Anita Zsurzsán portray the uprising as an authentic working-class revolution, presenting Soviet intervention as the suppression of a movement for socialist democracy. Their argument, however, elevates the genuine aspirations of sections of the Hungarian working class into the defining character of the entire uprising, while minimizing the political forces that sought to turn the crisis towards the dismantling of socialism. The serious mistakes committed under Mátyás Rákosi cannot be ignored. Economic imbalances, bureaucratic arbitrariness, coercive practices and weaknesses in the relationship between the Hungarian Workers’ Party and the masses had generated widespread dissatisfaction, including among industrial workers. These problems demanded correction, not concealment. But the crisis was aggravated by another decisive factor: the advance of opportunism and revisionism within the communist movement itself. The ideological confusion following the 20th Congress of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, particularly Khrushchev’s denunciation of Stalin, contributed to the weakening of revolutionary principles and encouraged political tendencies that increasingly questioned the foundations of socialist power. In Hungary, the revisionist current associated with Imre Nagy presented its political orientation as a democratic renewal of socialism. Under slogans promising a more national and supposedly democratic socialist system, it blurred the distinction between correcting the shortcomings of socialist construction and dismantling its political foundations. This confusion did not remain confined to party leadership circles. It also influenced sections of the working class, particularly those already disillusioned by economic difficulties and bureaucratic practices. Workers who sincerely wanted to improve socialism could therefore find themselves supporting political developments whose consequences they neither anticipated nor desired. This is essential to understanding the workers’ councils, which occupy such a central place in Jacobin’s argument. The authors emphasize their emergence in industrial centres such as Csepel, Miskolc and Dunapentele, presenting them as evidence that the uprising was fundamentally socialist. They also point to workers who identified their cause with socialism, opposed fascist excesses and demanded greater participation in political and economic decisions. These facts establish genuine working-class participation, but do not, by themselves, the class character of the entire uprising. The councils were politically heterogeneous, combining demands for workplace democracy and the preservation of socialist property with opposition to Soviet troops and calls for far-reaching political changes. Even after November 4, workers continued striking and organizing against the intervention and the government headed by János Kádár. Such resistance reflected genuine grievances, but also the depth of the political confusion into which the crisis had developed. A worker could sincerely believe he was fighting for socialism while supporting forces and political demands that objectively weakened socialist power. That is precisely why opportunism is so dangerous: it can turn legitimate dissatisfaction into support for a political course fundamentally opposed to the interests it claims to defend. Meanwhile, the uprising was moving far beyond demands for reform. Bourgeois political parties re-emerged, armed anti-communist groups gained ground, state institutions disintegrated and Nagy announced Hungary’s withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact. The struggle had become one over the country’s political orientation and the survival of its socialist system. The violence accompanying these developments cannot be overlooked. On October 30, armed insurgents attacked the headquarters of the Hungarian Workers’ Party in Budapest’s Republic Square. Captured defenders were brutally murdered, and their bodies subjected to public humiliation. These atrocities, documented by Western photographers, exposed the presence of forces prepared to physically eliminate communists. Imperialism, for its part, did not have to manufacture the crisis. The United States and its allies could exploit existing contradictions, encourage anti-Soviet sentiments and promote political developments favourable to the weakening of socialism. Through propaganda, political pressure and psychological warfare, Western imperialism sought to turn Hungary’s internal crisis into an opportunity to undermine socialist power and open the road towards capitalist restoration. This does not mean that every protester was an imperialist agent or that Washington directed every armed group. The danger arose precisely because genuine popular discontent, revisionist disorientation and organized counterrevolution became intertwined. It was under these circumstances that the Soviet intervention of November 4 took place. No communist should regard the entry of Soviet troops into a socialist country, with the suffering and loss of life it entailed, as something desirable. It was a painful development , reflecting both the gravity of the crisis and the failure to resolve its contradictions politically. By early November, the breakdown of established authority, armed anti-communist violence and the growing influence of counterrevolutionary forces had created the danger of prolonged internal conflict, potentially leading to civil war and further bloodshed. The Soviet leadership faced an exceptionally difficult decision. While Jacobin emphasizes Moscow’s fear of a workers’ revolution from below, the danger of counterrevolutionary forces consolidating power made intervention appear necessary from the standpoint of defending socialism. It was an odious necessity, a bitter decision whose human cost should neither be concealed nor separated from the circumstances that produced it. The Kádár government subsequently faced considerable resistance, including from workers’ councils whose leaders were subjected to arrests and other coercive measures. These developments cannot simply be explained away. Yet neither do they establish that a victory of the uprising would have produced a more democratic socialism rather than a fundamentally different political and social order. The following decades of socialist construction in Hungary, with significant advances in industry, agriculture, education, healthcare and living standards, also belong to the historical record. They cannot be erased from the assessment of the country’s post-1956 development. There is, moreover, a revealing contradiction in Jacobin’s interpretation. The authors criticize the appropriation of 1956 by Viktor Orbán’s nationalist right. Yet their own reading shares with the dominant bourgeois interpretation a crucial emphasis: the struggle against Soviet-backed socialist power becomes the central narrative of emancipation, even if the political objectives attributed to that struggle are fundamentally different. But Jacobin’s familiar social-democratic, anti-Soviet framework allows the authors to recognize the mistakes of socialist construction while overlooking the contradiction at the heart of their argument: the socialist aspirations of sections of the working class did not necessarily coincide with the political direction of the forces gaining influence in the uprising. The restoration of capitalism in Hungary in 1989–1990 offers another historical lesson. It was facilitated not primarily by foreign military intervention, but by the advance of opportunist and revisionist forces within the ruling party itself, whose political course contributed to the dismantling of socialism. Although the circumstances were different, this later experience demonstrated how the weakening of revolutionary principles and the transformation of communist parties from within could open the road to capitalist restoration. The tragedy of 1956 was not that Hungarian workers demanded improvements in their lives or greater participation in socialist administration. Such demands deserved serious attention. The tragedy was that genuine grievances were exploited amid deep political confusion, allowing counterrevolutionary forces to gain ground and placing socialist power in mortal danger. The decisive question is therefore not whether workers participated in the uprising, nor whether many of them sincerely believed they were defending socialism. They did. The question is which political forces were gaining the upper hand, whose class interests were being advanced and what social order their victory would have made possible. By avoiding that fundamental distinction, Jacobin turns a contradictory counterrevolutionary crisis into a romanticized tale of proletarian emancipation. Its interpretation may conform to the magazine’s longstanding hostility towards Soviet socialism, but it offers little understanding of the actual lessons of Hungary in 1956. ________________________ -Nikos Mottas is the Editor-in-Chief of In Defense of Communism .
