articles.title: “U.S. Policy Will Change Before Cubans Tire of Defending Our Sovereignty”: Cuban Foreign Minister
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: CUBADEBATE November 5, 2026 N.Y. Times Journalist Jack Nicas: What is the status of the talks between your government and the United States? When was the last time you spoke, and who is involved? Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez Parrilla: Yes, the talks continue, but without significant results or much progress. Given the coercive nature of the policy that the United States government is currently applying very intensely against Cuba, and given that it is very difficult for talks to progress when they are constantly accompanied by threats and the application of unilateral coercive measures—military threats, threats of a military nature, or even fuel blockades, which are equivalent to a naval blockade, an act of war—and a series of actions that constitute an act of collective punishment under International Law. Therefore, our willingness to continue these talks remains, with the aim of finding solutions to bilateral issues based on international law, sovereign equality, on an equal footing, without interference in internal affairs, and on the basis of mutual respect and reciprocal benefit. I need not go into too much detail, but I confirm that talks have taken place and that the Cuban side remains willing to continue. Journalist : I understand you don’t want to go into some specific details, but what are the channels like, to understand, are they face-to-face conversations or by phone, what are they like? Minister: Yes, as I was saying, I preferred not to go into details. These are political-level talks in which the Cuban side has maintained a constant willingness to move forward in resolving bilateral problems, some of them long-standing and others stemming from the hardening of the US government’s policy against Cuba, which is causing extraordinary humanitarian damage. Journalist: Except that your Chargé d’Affaires in Washington said there are channels such as meetings, calls, and WhatsApp messages. Can you confirm that? Minister: If the Chargé d’Affaires said so, I don’t need to confirm it. Journalist: Have you spoken this month, in October? Minister: I told him I preferred not to go into details, but talks have been ongoing for some time without major results and I hope they will continue. Journalist: The White House has said there needs to be political change. Your administration has made it clear that this isn’t going to happen and that it’s not appropriate to discuss such a matter. Where is there room for negotiation? What, if anything, is your administration willing to concede? Minister: Imagine if the Cuban government were to say that for talks with the United States to take place, there must be political change in the United States. Furthermore, the United States government does not apply a single standard on this issue because it maintains excellent relations with countries that have governments, political systems, and electoral systems—or even lack them altogether—completely different from U.S. standards. Third, no political difference could justify a siege like the one being waged against Cuba today. No political difference could be a sufficient pretext for imposing a fuel blockade against a small, peace-loving nation; and no political reason could justify acts of collective punishment that cause harm, pain, suffering, and anguish to all Cuban families. I can tell you that we, too, have concerns regarding the American political system. We don’t like their model of democracy, but we persist in the idea of a plurality of political models, a plurality of democratic models, based on the plurality of cultures that exist on the planet. We do not agree with the idea of a single way of thinking, a single model, a single culture, and even less so that this culture should be modeled on the dysfunctional American democracy. But this is not a matter for our bilateral discussions. It should not be an obstacle to making progress in resolving long-standing or more recent bilateral issues. For example, Cuba has always been willing to address issues that are of interest and benefit to the national interest of the United States and especially to the American people. For example, Cuba has provided and will continue to provide its full cooperation in law enforcement and compliance, in relation to national or joint efforts against terrorism, drug trafficking, human trafficking, and international organized crime, and in support of a satisfactory migration relationship between the two countries. There are numerous areas, well, there are still 22 bilateral cooperation agreements in force in areas that are of the greatest interest to both nations and should be of the greatest interest to both governments, and we are fully prepared to continue efforts in that regard. For example, in the area of counterterrorism, Cuba has made significant efforts in relation to the latest act of terrorism against Cuba, which was the attempted infiltration of Cuban territory by a heavily armed terrorist cell equipped with weapons of war, explosives, and communications equipment. We have offered the United States government a joint investigation into this matter. And there are long-standing issues, such as the matter of mutual compensation, stemming from the nationalizations of U.S. properties in Cuba, carried out under both Cuban and U.S. law. These nationalizations were recognized by the U.S. Supreme Court in the Sabatino case, for example, as lawful, but the owners were unable to receive compensation precisely because of the obstacles and historical antagonism of the U.S. government. And in Cuba, there are also rulings by Cuban courts demanding compensation from the U.S. government for economic and human damages suffered by Cuba during these 60 years of bilateral conflict. Journalist: I think your position is very reasonable, but the situation is that the White House isn’t necessarily very reasonable in this situation, so it’s clear they’re asking for political changes, things you don’t want to discuss. It seems like the things on the table for you are about, well, aid on terrorism, things like that, also maybe reparations, and maybe economic reforms. Are they asking for specific things regarding political or economic changes right now, or do they seem satisfied with these concessions on terrorism, things like that? Minister: Well, it’s difficult to say; that would be a good question for the U.S. side. But I can tell you that Cuba is currently engaged in very important changes to its economic model. These changes are not the result of talks or requests from the U.S. government, but rather stem from our own realities and our desire to ensure the well-being and prosperity of our people. Of course, the international economic environment has become very challenging due to global changes; and secondly, because the Cuban economy must necessarily adapt to this economic war being waged by the U.S. government. But I have always thought that in the area of economic relations, investment, travel – I don’t say tourism because it is prohibited by US law – in relations between US citizens and Cuba, in the area of health, in the area of the biomedical or pharmaceutical industry and in others, there are great possibilities to advance for the benefit of both peoples. A few months ago, Cuba launched a program of changes to its economic model, which are not aimed at fulfilling any requests in this regard, but which open up additional opportunities for US companies to do business with Cuban counterparts. These changes will take into account the interests of U.S. companies based on their merit and competitiveness. In other words, there will be neither privileges nor discrimination for U.S. companies that wish to take advantage of this opportunity. In 2018, over 600,000 Americans and over 400,000 Cubans residing in the United States traveled to Cuba. A thriving private industry developed around these trips, but it later suffered the consequences of the cessation and prohibition of these operations. More recently, the United States government, as it does almost every other Thursday, has taken decisions that further restrict Americans’ right to travel freely, particularly their right to travel to our country, by eliminating certain licenses that, until now, allowed such travel, albeit in a very limited way. In recent years, Cuba has experienced significant growth in its private sector, with a rise in small and medium-sized enterprises that are entirely privately owned. Extensive opportunities have opened up for Cubans living abroad, including in the United States, to participate in these businesses, and ample opportunities are being offered to foreign investors. The United States should not be allowed to control sectors of the Cuban economy to the detriment of its international competitors in this area, but the presence of its companies, which we recognize as competitive, would be welcome in the Cuban economy. For example, in the health and biomedical-pharmaceutical sectors, Cuba also has comparative advantages. It has some therapeutic vaccines, in some cases unique or among the most successful, for treating head, neck, and lung cancer. It has a treatment unique in the world for diabetes, particularly for preventing amputations resulting from diabetic foot ulcers. It has very innovative medications for treating degenerative neurological diseases, including Alzheimer’s, and has a wide range of treatments and experience in the production of new technologies, possessing technologies that are currently unique. Why not encourage this cooperation? Why deprive Americans of these options that we know are of interest to American companies, or even to patient associations, medical associations, or groups of people? Secondly, what political pretext could justify preventing a Cuban child with cancer from accessing the best treatments, or even the specific, appropriate treatment, which in some cases is exclusively American and protected by American patents? How can we prevent a newborn from accessing less invasive treatments for genetic heart conditions using American medical devices, technologies, or equipment that are virtually exclusive to the world? There is no way to justify that, in a politically motivated manner, which is the core of this administration’s US policy against Cuba, which is to create despair, anguish, suffering, and pain in the population with the aim of destabilizing the country and provoking a regime change. I don’t know if you are familiar with a 1960 memorandum from an Under Secretary of State in the Eisenhower administration, Lester Mallory. I suggest you look it up. It was a classified document for 30 years, but it remains the main orientation of US policy against Cuba, which recognizes the majority support of the Cuban people for the constitutional order that has been established in several free and universal referendums, because in Cuba the Constitution and fundamental laws are submitted to popular referendum and have been freely and sovereignly chosen by our people. That memorandum recognizes that the way to alienate the majority consensus of the Cuban people is precisely by causing suffering, and that this is what allows us to affirm in a technical-legal, not rhetorical, way that the economic, commercial and financial blockade imposed against Cuba is classified as an act of genocide according to the Geneva Convention and is classified as an act of collective punishment according to International Law, International Human Rights Law or even International Humanitarian Law, which is used only in times of military conflict. The fuel blockade is tantamount to a hostile act, an act of war under International Humanitarian Law, causing devastating humanitarian damage. For example, Cuba’s health indicators are currently comparable to those of developed countries, yet they reflect these impacts. Infant mortality—that is, the mortality rate of children under five years of age born alive, which is considered one of the most representative indicators of human development and the health and well-being of a population—is currently 9.9 per 1,000 live births. This is comparable to developed countries, but this rate has doubled in recent years due to these extreme blockade measures, because our regular rate was around 4 per 1,000 live births. The life expectancy of children with cancer in Cuba was among the highest in the world, at 85%, but it has fallen to 65%. Health indicators show a decline in the levels of timely and early immunization of children against communicable diseases, in the monitoring of pregnant women (with studies that are very thorough in Cuba), and in the country’s overall mortality data, all of which are effects of this cruel and inhumane policy. There could be highly beneficial alliances between U.S. institutions and Cuban institutions, which are among the most competitive in the world in the biomedical and pharmaceutical fields, to cooperate on treatments for both communicable and non-communicable diseases. Cuba was able to produce five COVID-19 vaccines in record time and with minimal resources, guaranteeing immunity for our population and achieving some of the best results in the world in confronting that pandemic. Journalist: The relationship between your country and the United States is very unequal, very, very unequal. The United States is much more powerful, much richer, much larger, and they are currently very aggressive toward you. They want political change, and you haven’t seen almost any allies coming to your aid. So it’s a very, very serious situation, and your people are suffering. So, what is your strategy for getting out of this situation? Minister: Well, imagine what the United States government would do if, 90 miles from the United States, there were a global superpower far larger than the United States, in the same proportion as the US economy, its Gross Domestic Product, its armed forces, its weapons capabilities, including the existence of nuclear weapons, its territory, and its technological development. It would be a country that obviously doesn’t exist today, precisely because I agree with you on the enormous disproportion between the power of a small nation, a small island state with a developing economy subject to these circumstances, and this great nuclear superpower. What would the policies of a government like this be under those circumstances? How would American democracy function under those circumstances? How would the US economy function if this enormous, imaginary superpower, controlling finance, technology, and the global economy, pursued a regime change policy against the United States? Secondly, we should also consider the situation of other countries in our region or any other region, or even developed countries, that were subjected to a siege like this for 60 years, or that for the last five or six years had been subjected to an extreme blockade like this, or that for almost a year had been prevented from receiving fuel supplies. How many countries would have withstood it? How many governments would have remained in place? Which countries could have avoided a humanitarian catastrophe? People dying en masse in the streets, widespread famine. Yet Cuba has had the capacity to prevent that, to resist that, and to do so without giving up. I, too, have heard politicians… Journalist: Excuse me, but with all due respect, I understand perfectly, and I think it’s very reasonable, and the question isn’t about the ethics of Americans. We’ve already written about what Americans are doing, creating suffering in Cuba, but the question is what their strategy is for getting out of this situation. Minister: Yes, and I am responding to you. I am responding in the sense of trying to help New York Times readers understand that very few countries on the planet would have been able to have this conversation today, almost a year after the policies that have been applied against Cuba were implemented, especially since January 3 of this year, and yet there has not been a humanitarian catastrophe in Cuba; we have been able to prevent it. The Cuban economy has not collapsed. The state remains effective because the effectiveness of a state must be measured considering these oppressive circumstances. And I was saying that I’ve noticed some US politicians, including the Secretary of State, for example, have been lowering expectations regarding immediate regime change in Cuba. First they said it would be in a few weeks, then they said it would be immediately after what happened in early January in South America, then they said as soon as there was a pause in the war against Iran, then they said it would be before summer, during the summer. Someone said in 30 days we will control the Cuban economy. The president said we will take Cuba, we will control Cuba, friendly or unfriendly, immediately. And yet, the Secretary of State now explains that patience and time are needed, that this is a supposed problem that has existed for many decades and cannot be solved quickly, and he has proclaimed, therefore, that the objective of this US administration is not immediate regime change, but rather that Cuba be on an irreversible path of approximation to US interests. So, given this situation, one has to ask oneself, well, what is the reason—and it’s a question I’m frequently asked—why Cuba has been able to withstand this unprecedented pressure, because there has never been a sanctions regime anywhere in the world, in history, like the one that has been historically applied against Cuba, nor has there ever been, nor is there now, another comprehensive system of blockade and unilateral coercive measures against any country like the one being applied against Cuba today. For example, there is currently no country being prevented from receiving fuel supplies, and not only fuel supplies, but also because action has been taken against shipping companies—that is, maritime transport companies—forcing them to renege on signed and paid contracts. Most of these shipments contain perishable and essential goods such as food, medicine, and medical devices, and the majority of these shipments were contracted by the private sector, by small and medium-sized private companies in Cuba. These goods are currently located in various ports around the world because, faced with threats and sanctions, the shipping companies refuse to honor their contracts and deliver the goods to Cuban ports. This has jeopardized, for example, the hemodialysis treatments in Cuba for more than 3,000 patients. Hemodialysis treatments are a matter of life or death and cannot be postponed, yet we have been able to resolve this issue. We have an economic program, as I mentioned before, which is part of our strategy not only for survival but also for the recovery of our economic growth. Its main objective is the well-being of the population, guaranteeing social justice and social coverage, ensuring that no family or individual is left destitute. However, it also significantly changes the economic model, which will remain socialist but opens up many new opportunities for private capital, foreign investors, and companies from different countries. We would like to invite American companies to participate in these opportunities. Secondly, Cuba is receiving extraordinary international solidarity that encourages us, and US policy against Cuba is suffering enormous discredit and international isolation. If our strategy weren’t working, why then, last January, after exhausting five or six years of extreme blockade measures, had a total energy blockade been declared? If our strategy and our state were ineffective, why had secondary sanctions been added in May against all countries with ties to Cuba? Why, every other Thursday, have new sanctions been applied—some unimaginable, some even designed to impede Cuba’s international cooperation with other countries, such as Cuba’s international medical cooperation with African and Caribbean nations, from which Cuba receives no income? Because Cuba is an exporter of medical services, but it also has cooperation programs from which it receives no benefit. In other words, why do all this if the Cuban strategy and the Cuban state are considered ineffective? The day after tomorrow, that is, tomorrow and the day after tomorrow, the United Nations General Assembly will consider the issue of the blockade against Cuba and I am sure that it will approve with a large majority vote a resolution demanding that the United States unconditionally end the blockade against Cuba. If our strategy and our situation were not effective, why would the United States have had to dedicate itself in recent months, since June and in recent weeks in particular, across the globe, to threatening governments, threatening foreign ministries, deploying its ambassadors everywhere, the Secretary of State sending documents? I have some of those documents in my possession; some I have already shown, others I will show now in the General Assembly. They are terribly threatening documents, not only against governments but even against their readers, their recipients, because they threaten them directly. They require very careful reading and very thorough consideration, under penalty of applying sanctions to the governments and to you, the recipient and your family. Journalist: So, Minister, it seems to me that the strategy then… Minister: If the strategy didn’t work, we wouldn’t be talking here today. Journalist : I understand , but what’s the strategy? Is it survival? Is it to last? Is it to wait until the United States gets tired of it . Minister: The United States’ policy toward Cuba is going to change. It will have to change. It’s inevitable that it will change. Journalist: Why? Minister: First, because American citizens oppose it. All the polls from 2026 and all the online conversation studies in the United States, particularly in English, reflect around 70% opposition to the energy blockade and collective punishment. I don’t know about the New York Times, but I frequently encounter the terms “fuel blockade” and “collective punishment” in the mainstream American press, which is a new phenomenon. This is not only reflected in Cuban statements, but also in the language of American journalists and other individuals. Secondly, because the majority of Cubans residing in the United States, although many of them do not vote, also oppose this policy of collective punishment or even military threat against my country, just like American citizens. Third, because it’s a very old policy that hasn’t yielded the slightest result. In other words, for 60 years this policy hasn’t moved the United States, or successive administrations, one iota toward the goals each of them has proclaimed. It’s a policy that has failed for 60 years. It is a policy that has been taken to extremes to practically warlike levels; it is an economic war that has lasted for almost a year, which has not advanced the United States one millimeter towards the regime change goals it proclaimed. Journalist: But politics has lasted quite a while too . Minister: A lot. Journalist: So the question is, it seems your strategy is to survive, to last, and you’re achieving that. But the question then is, how much longer can you survive? Minister: Fourth, the policy will have to change because it runs counter to the national interest of the United States. What could the national interest of the United States possibly be regarding Cuba? To destabilize the Caribbean Basin? To destabilize the area where there are enormous oil investments by the United States and other regional partners in the Caribbean Basin? To destabilize the important maritime trade routes that supply the ports of the eastern United States? To destabilize the Caribbean and Central America? To generate an uncontrolled wave of migration to the United States? If the Cuban economy were to collapse, what would happen the next day? What would happen in relation to the United States? But I am answering your question, although you may think I am going on for too long, and perhaps you are in a hurry. But as I was saying, it contradicts the national interest of the United States. Furthermore, it only discredits and isolates the United States in terms of foreign policy. It undermines the United States’ national interest in the Americas and the Caribbean region. So, it must be acknowledged that, in these 60 years, up to today, October 26, the United States’ policy against Cuba has not worked, while Cuba’s policy of resistance and adaptation to that aggression has worked and has been successful. For how long? For as long as it takes. The United States’ policy will change sooner than we Cubans will tire of defending our independence, our sovereignty, our territorial integrity. This is an issue that dates back more than 100 years. In other words, this conflict did not begin with the Cuban Revolution. The United States’ desire to seize and dominate Cuba dates back to the 19th century. Journalist: Very well. I’m in no hurry, it’s just that he’s going to tell me… Minister: It’s the friend who’s in a hurry… I understand. Journalist: And it’s very important to get some specific and clear answers to get a story about that. Because five months ago your government said that Cuba’s oil had run out, but now in October you’re operating. Where is the oil coming from, and how much more? Minister: Well, almost half of the oil that the Cuban economy needs is produced in Cuba. We produce a crude oil that is very heavy and has a high sulfur content, which we couldn’t refine. Part of our strategy has been to develop our own refining technology. This is a fact. Another fact is that we have opened up possibilities for the private sector to import fuel, which are small because the United States government prevents the private sector from importing larger quantities of fuel, applying restriction after restriction and forcing them to do so only in very small, very limited quantities and at exorbitant prices. Journalist: How do you feel about receiving oil from the United States? Does it create a dependency? Minister: Perfectly. Well, it’s an idea that hasn’t been considered because there seems to be no danger of the Cuban economy becoming dependent on US fuel because US regulations prevent that possibility; they fiercely prevent it to this day. But what I want to tell you is that for us, having a presence on equal footing with European and other global companies in the Cuban economy would be desirable. Regarding energy, one factor that has allowed us to survive, and not only survive but also increase our capacity, is that despite the US embargo, we have achieved significant development in renewable energy, particularly photovoltaics, in record time. Today, during daylight hours, more than half of Cuba’s electricity generation comes from photovoltaic sources. So, that’s another factor in our adaptation. Journalist: Very well. Two more questions. The other thing is, are you counting on or expecting the US midterm elections to change your situation? Minister: That would be difficult to answer. First, the question is somewhat hypothetical because we don’t know the outcome of the election until the taxpayers, the American voters, cast their ballots in the first days of November. Second, because we would have to see how American democracy will function under whatever circumstances arise, whatever the possible results. But today it is a reality that the majority of American voters and the majority of American taxpayers oppose this policy. Hopefully, in any case, both the government and Congress will take into account the will of the American people. We will have to wait and see. Journalist : Isn’t this vote part of your hope or strategy that the situation will change? Minister: No, a matter that is entirely internal to the United States cannot be a variable in our strategy. Journalist: And finally, of course, you’ve seen this message from Rubio in which they’re looking for informants for the CIA. What do you think of a strategy that seeks informants in that way? And also this morning, the United States Ambassador to Cuba met with the Armed Forces, and they said there’s a lot to discuss regarding Cuba. What’s your opinion, what’s your reaction? Minister: Well, we would have to ask our American counterparts. It is known that, at the time, in addition to diplomatic talks with the State Department, there was contact between the U.S. and Cuban armed forces and between the Central Intelligence Agency and its Cuban counterparts. The truth is, I have no idea what the Secretary of State is trying to achieve with these publications, which frankly don’t seem serious at all; they seem a bit childish. And the truth is, I can’t understand why the Secretary of State is referring to public instructions from an intelligence agency asking Cubans to recruit them en masse and giving them directions that seem more like something out of a James Bond movie than reality. Journalist: To say those things publicly, do you think they’re trying to psychologically manipulate you or mess with you guys in some way? Minister: There is an unconventional war being waged against Cuba that has been part of these past 60 years. A war that today they call cognitive or fourth- or fifth-generation warfare, which they intend to wage not in a physical theater of operations, but now not only in cyberspace but also in people’s minds, in their very being. It won’t work because the Cuban people have, first of all, a high level of education. Secondly, because they have a very high level of information, and thirdly, because they have a high level of political awareness. They recognize who is responsible for the harm they are suffering, the consequences they are enduring, and the real causes of their suffering, anguish, and deprivation. They enjoy broad, intergenerational consensus at the social level. They feel that they are participating in the search for solutions, in the search for ways out, despite the Secretary of State’s repeated assertions that every time Cuba finds a way out, every time there is a valve, the US government will shut it down, will cut it off. But we Cubans feel like we’re participating in this process because Cuban culture is native, it’s powerful, because the idea of Cuban independence and sovereignty is practically ingrained, an essential part of our culture. The determination to defend our territorial integrity, our homeland, to the very end, at the grassroots level, is a cultural matter, shared by the vast majority of our population. But it is true that there is a very intense cognitive war against our country that is as illegal and inhumane as the fuel blockade or collective punishment or preventing shipping companies from bringing their merchandise to our country. Journalist: Very well, thank you very much. Do you have a little more time? One more question, or what? Minister: One more. Journalist : Well, about privatization. Minister: Excuse me? Journalist: On privatization. Minister: Privatization. Journalist: Thank you. “Privatization, privatization.” I believe his government calls the reforms “flexibilization,” not privatization. But it seems Cuba is selling shares in state-owned companies to Cubans and foreigners, and several other things are being privatized—gas stations and pharmacies are now privately owned. So, will this make Cuba cease to be communist, or is this a real change, or is it just temporary? How should we think about these economic reforms? Is this a real change? Minister: How would you describe a communist economy? Journalist: Well, an economy that the State has basically total control over. Minister: Well, in communism there is supposed to be no state. Journalist: Is there no state in communism? Minister: That’s what Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels wrote, and that’s what Marxists think. Journalist: You know much better than I do. Minister: No, because you’re asking from a place of prejudice or a slogan—which I hope hasn’t influenced the New York Times—that labels Cuba as communist: “Communist Cuba,” “a communist regime,” “a communist economy.” This is completely wrong from both a theoretical and practical standpoint. You could then ask about a socialist Cuba, a socialist economy, and so on. Journalist: Isn’t Cuba communist? Minister: Cuba is not communist, nor could it be. Just as there has never been, nor is there today, any communist state on the planet. Secondly, yes, there are socialist states. There are some with which the current US government has an excellent relationship. There are Asian socialist states with which the United States has a very intense economic, commercial, and investment relationship. They have a true economic interdependence, and I think that’s perfectly fine. And that highlights once again the double standard in American politics, which has excellent relations with other socialist countries or socialist states and also has excellent relations with other countries that are not socialist, but which have a political system that has nothing to do with so-called American democracy. Not only because there is no pluralism of political parties, but because there are none at all, for example. So, what I mean is that the profound economic changes being introduced in Cuba, the profound changes in the Cuban economic model, as I mentioned before, will continue to be focused on the well-being of the population, particularly families and people with lower incomes. It will continue to be centered on social policies with universal coverage, universal protection for our population, which is what has brought us to this point, but these policies entail significant modifications, especially in the distribution of financial and material resources in the country. This includes the continued development of the private sector in Cuba, which is gradually increasing its weight in the Cuban economy. This includes new facilities, incentives, and new conditions—more advantageous conditions, I would say—for foreign counterparties, for direct capital investment in Cuba, for the management of Cuban assets, and for leveraging the comparative advantages that Cuba offers to foreign counterparties. But the Cuban economy will remain socialist. The Cuban model will remain socialist. Like some very successful Asian socialist economies with close economic ties to the United States, the well-being and dignity of human beings will always remain fundamental. But you are right that privatizing some state-owned enterprises is not out of the question, as is already happening to some extent. Part of that process is the conversion to equity capital or contributions from corporations and state-owned enterprises. In some sectors, as everywhere in the world, government entities will seek to acquire controlling shares. State-owned enterprises will also seek to acquire controlling shares. This is the case, for example, with US railroads, and it also occurs in Switzerland and other sectors in Europe, but it does indeed include additional options for the private sector. But it would be an exaggeration to call this set of changes, this transformation, a privatization process because it is not essentially that. It includes privatizations, but privatization is not what distinguishes the transformation of the economic model, which will continue to plan the distribution of resources through the market with non-administrative financial levers and will give the market an even greater role in formulating economic policies and in the economic model itself. Journalist: Very good, very helpful. I understand better now. Is there anything else that…? Minister: Thank you very much. Journalist: Thank you very much. ********* Translation by Walter Lippmann. Full transcript of the statements made by Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla to journalist Jack Nicas, The New York Times: http://www.cubadebate.cu/especiales/2026/11/05/bruno-rodriguez-antes-cambiara-la-politica-de-ee-uu-que-los-cubanos-nos-cansemos-de-defender-nuestra-soberania/ The post “U.S. Policy Will Change Before Cubans Tire of Defending Our Sovereignty”: Cuban Foreign Minister appeared first on MLToday .

articles.title: Black Faces in High Place Are Still Not Going to Save Us
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By Margaret Kimberley, BAR Exec. Editor & Senior Columnist November 11, 2026 Black Agenda Report The recent midterm elections have brought more Black people to high elected office, but for 20 years, Black Agenda Report has warned about the dangers of the Black misleadership class. “Just look at the black proponents of Cop City in Atlanta’s leadership class. Black faces in high places are not going to save us.” – Dr. Ruha Benjamin, June 2024 It is accurate to say that the results of the November 3 midterm elections in the United States were quite historic. Not only did republican states like Texas and Kansas reject their long-time affiliation with republicans and instead elect democrats, but Black people were elected to statewide offices in record numbers. Four Black governors were newly elected: Byron Donalds in Florida, David Crowley in Wisconsin, Aaron Ford in Nevada, and Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia. Juliana Stratton was elected to the Senate in Illinois, and while votes are still being counted, Scott Colom is in the lead in a Mississippi Senate race. The U.S. Senate and the House of Representatives now both have Democratic Party majorities, and Donald Trump, while still in possession of significant presidential powers, is definitely on the back foot. Yet in its 20 years of publication, Black Agenda Report has never been a proponent of reveling in the success of Black faces in high places. Doing so is a recipe for political disenfranchisement precisely because a victory in elected office usually comes at the expense of the masses of Black people. Support from the donor class and those institutions whose needs are antithetical to those of the people is a prerequisite for gaining high office. Yet the lure and power of representation remain strong. It isn’t difficult to understand how this legacy of decades of Jim Crow segregation and anti-Black public policy makes the very presence of Black people in positions of prominence so attractive, particularly when southern states are part of this turn of political events and Keisha Lance Bottoms prepares to become governor of Georgia in the heart of Dixie, or that Congressional Black Caucus member Hakeem Jeffries is poised to become Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives. Bottoms and Jeffries both offer cautionary tales about the Black face in the high places, which still electrifies so many of our people. Bottoms was part of that generation of Black mayors of Atlanta who took office after Maynard Jackson began this trajectory of white-approved leadership in the 1970s. The city that was said to be “too busy to hate” was actually one in which rich white people decided that having Black mayors front for their interests was the most expedient course of action. In April 2021, Bottoms announced a plan for what she called a public safety training center. The euphemism Cop City was a more accurate moniker, and the announcement, which came less than one year after protests over the killing of George Floyd and of Rayshard Brooks in Atlanta, was not coincidental. The city of Atlanta pledged $90 million in public funds for Cop City when most residents were opposed to the project. An additional $60 million was pledged by the Atlanta Police Foundation (APF), which is controlled by people like billionaire Arthur Blank . Blank is a co-founder of the Home Depot chain of houseware stores and owner of the Atlanta Falcons football team. Corporations such as Delta Airlines, Coca-Cola, Bank of America, and Cox Communications are also APF funders. Blank is now a member of Bottoms’ transition team. At the behest of Blank and his ilk, Bottoms and her predecessor, current mayor Andre Dickens, pushed through the project while keeping a referendum on Cop City off the ballot. Opposition had resulted in one protester being shot to death by police, and 60 others were charged with RICO conspiracy, so dedicated were Atlanta’s ruling class to making Cop City a reality. They succeeded in doing so. Bottoms’ gubernatorial race victory was a reward for her service. Hakeem Jeffries will in all likelihood become Speaker of the House. Like Bottoms and other elected officials, he owes his position as Democratic Party leader to the Israel lobby, big pharma, financial services, and the military-industrial complex. The list is not surprising. Those are the interests with the most money to spend. Jeffries, though, is less skilled than Bottoms and makes clear who is pulling his strings. Of course no one can climb the congressional ladder to a leadership position without supporting Israel. But Jeffries couldn’t make that support clear without sounding like Alabama governor George Wallace , who famously said, “Segregation today, segregation tomorrow, segregation forever.” In a 2014 speech, before he even became leader, the hapless Jeffries proclaimed , “Israel today, Israel tomorrow, Israel forever!” This columnist may sneer, but he won the audition and should soon be Speaker of the House after proving his willingness to be servile to the right people. Lest we forget, he recently met with Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner for reasons which we will never know. Regardless of the details, Jeffries showed a shocking lack of shrewdness in acceding to the request of a rich donor who remained nameless. His explanation that he and Kushner talked about affordability rings quite hollow. The sorry episode shows how business is done and for whom. For all of its 20 years of existence, Black Agenda Report contributors have spoken of the opportunistic Black misleadership class. Bottoms and Jeffries exemplify this cohort, and their elevations to positions of power give Black people nothing except misguided feelings of pride. We are not saved by mayors, governors, senators, or Speakers of the House. They are not accountable to the people. They answer to the Arthur Blanks of the world. Atlanta’s rich white people are the political class writ large. They and their friends ensure protection for themselves by putting compliant people like Bottoms and Jeffries in office, who in turn use the sincere feelings of Black people for their own benefit. We have seen this movie many times, and we know the ending. Black faces in high places are still not going to save us. -Margaret Kimberley is the author of Prejudential: Black America and the Presidents . articles.title: Sheinbaum Pursues Failed Neo-liberal Policies, Says Mexican Communist Leader
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By Tim Pelzer September 21, 2026 The Guardian (Australia) MEXICO CITY – The social democratic government of Claudia Sheinbaum is continuing the same failed neo-liberal policies of the previous Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador administration, said Angel Chavez, member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of Mexico (PCM) in an interview. Instead of diversifying export markets and strengthening national production, the Sheinbaum National Regeneration Movement (MORENA) government is trying to save and extend the US, Mexico, Canada Agreement ( USMCA) for another 16 years, a free trade pact that replaced NAFTA in 2020. “The deal primarily benefits the monopolies in the three member countries and has limited the country’s independence. The agreement tells each country what they can buy and sell. In the past Mexico was self-sufficient in corn — an important component of the diet — now it must import genetically modified corn from the US”, he said in a interview. When the free trade agreement was first signed in 1994, it ruined Mexican agriculture by allowing the US to flood the market with cheap corn, wheat and other products, bankrupting many farmers and impoverishing the countryside. The USMCA has halted the country’s economic development and turned Mexico into a low-wage maquiladora , dominated by foreign companies that import raw materials or components duty free, assemble them and then re-export finished products to the US and Canada. These plants, which employ millions of Mexicans and form a major part of the country’s manufacturing sector, take advantage of low wages and a six-day work week in Mexico. In the past the Mexican left opposed free trade with the US but now MORENA supports it, he said. Chavez complained the Sheinbaum government has also caved in to US demands to keep Chinese investment out of Mexico. “The USMCA even allows North American inspectors into factories to decide if a union meeting is legal”, claimed Chavez. The PCM opposes the Sheinbaum government’s attempts to save the USMCA and wants Mexico to pull out of the agreement. “MORENA does not want to overthrow capitalism but instead promised that it wanted to reform it and make it more beautiful through reforms, but now it does not want to even do that”, complained Chavez. During the 1980s and 1990s right-wing PRI and PAN [PRI and PAN are Mexican bourgeois parties] governments privatized hundreds of companies for well below their market value. “The first MORENA government of Lopez Obrador never re-nationalized these companies. Sheinbaum continues with his program.” MORENA`s approach to mass youth unemployment is a program called “Young People Constructing the Future”, started by Lopez Obrador in 2019 when he was first elected. “The government pays the wages of 3.5 million young people each year who work for private companies, providing free labor to capitalists at taxpayers’ expense,“ lamented Chavez. Workers are paid the minimum wage of 9,500 pesos per month and employers are not obligated to continue employing them after one year. He also challenged MORENA`s claim it has raised the minimum salary by 250% since 2019. “This is only a decree and has not been enforced. In many cases the government does not even obligate employers to pay the minimum wage.” When asked if MORENA governments have reduced poverty through the introduction of new social programs, he said that high inflation has been undermining these programs. He said that monopolies have been raising prices for basic goods, making it impossible to reduce poverty levels in the country. “These social programs were introduced primarily to win votes for MORENA and buy social peace and stability”. He said the country still has 50 million poor people [Mexico’s population is an estimated 133 million] and suffers from mass unemployment, compelling 55% of the labor force to work in the informal sector such as selling goods or food on the street because there is no unemployment insurance or welfare. “These conditions have force many Mexicans to migrate to the US and Canada,” he said. He is also critical of Sheinbaum for not protecting the 10 million Mexican immigrants living in the US. Recently it was reported that 18 Mexicans have died in ICE detention centers. “The government has not protested or did anything to help migrants. Instead it is helping the US deport immigrants back to Mexico.” The MORENA party government also stopped shipping oil to Cuba, helping to worsen the US blockade, lamented Chavez. Chavez said the PCM was not able to get its electoral registration back this year because of rules designed to keep opposition parties off the ballot. Mexican electoral authorities require a new party to submit 350 thousand signatures and hold costly assemblies in all 31 states, which proved impossible for the PCM to meet. He said MORENA has not expressed any intention to change these rules. Since its refounding in 1994, the PCM has been unable to regain its former electoral registration that it was granted in 1978. The party ran candidates in 1979, winning 5.4 % of the vote and electing 18 deputies to the National Parliament, becoming the third largest party in the country. In 1981, party members dissolved the party to form the Mexican Unified Socialist Party (PMS). In 1988, the PMS dissolved and formed the Democratic Revolution Party (PRD). The PRD – to which Lopez Obrador belonged during the first part of his political career, and which he abandoned to form MORENA in 2011 – inherited the PCM`s electoral registration and property. Denied ballot access for the 2024 elections, the PCM ran Marco Vinicio Davila for president as well as several candidates for state governor as write-in candidates – including Angel Chavez in Mexico City — which is allowed by the Mexican constitution. PCM candidates received 85,000 write-in votes and probably more since the party has evidence that many votes were marked as null. Chavez characterized the party’s electoral campaign as successful, especially the presidential race, despite a media blackout by the national television networks. He said Vinicio Davila traveled the country speaking at meetings, distributing tens of thousands of leaflets with volunteers, door knocking and giving interviews to media. “Marco became well know across the country”, remarked Chavez. “While l was campaigning with Marco in Mexico City where l was the candidate for governor, l remember people constantly approaching Marco on the street to speak with him.” Until the party can get back its electoral registration, Chavez said the PCM will continue running write-in candidates to offer a socialist alternative to the working class. articles.title: The Flight of Flávio Bolsonaro and the Maneuvers of the Empire
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: Political Note of the Brazilian Communist Party (PCB) October 30, 2026 In defense of the legitimacy of the electoral result and of popular mobilization against fascism, imperialism and neoliberalism! For People’s Power! Lula’s victory in the presidential elections against Flávio Bolsonaro represented a hard blow against the Brazilian far right and the pretensions of US imperialism to expand its dominion over Latin America. However, the political scenario remains quite adverse for the Brazilian working class. The composition of the National Congress, with a conservative majority committed to the neoliberal agenda and to sectors linked to the neofascist project, demonstrates that the battle against the far right will still be long and will require permanent mobilization and unity of action to defend the rights already won and to advance in the conquest of new demands. This conjuncture becomes even more serious in the face of Flávio Bolsonaro’s flight to the United States and the possible consequences of this episode for Brazil, even taking into account his pathetic letter, in which he calls himself president-elect of Brazil. The flight of the defeated candidate constitutes an event of enormous political gravity, whose significance goes beyond Brazilian borders. His search for protection on US territory, in the face of the investigations and accusations involving his crimes, cannot be interpreted as an isolated episode, but must be understood in the context of the historical relations between imperialism and the reactionary Latin American oligarchies. Over the course of decades, the United States has harbored and protected authoritarian politicians, coup conspirators and representatives of the dominant classes committed to its strategic interests. US imperialism, which seeks to present itself as a defender of democracy and freedom, does not hesitate to harbor and protect the most reactionary elements in Latin America when its economic and geopolitical interests are at stake. The protection given by Donald Trump’s government to Flávio Bolsonaro represents yet another manifestation of this policy of interference in the internal affairs of Latin American countries. It would not be surprising if Washington sought to turn the situation of the defeated candidate into an instrument of pressure against Brazil, using accusations of political persecution to attack the Supreme Federal Court, question the legitimacy of the electoral result and fuel new campaigns to destabilize the Brazilian government. The use of representatives of the Latin American far right as instruments of US foreign policy constitutes a historically known practice, especially when these sectors demonstrate a willingness to subordinate the sovereignty of their countries to the interests of imperialism. Flávio Bolsonaro’s flight could be used by the US government as a pretext to accuse Brazilian institutions of persecution and authoritarianism, intensifying Donald Trump’s pressures against national sovereignty and encouraging attacks on democratic institutions and the federal government. In this sense, the Brazilian Communist Party (PCB) reaffirms the need for a rigorous investigation of the accusations against the Bolsonaro clan, its allies, financiers and possible accomplices, with the due accountability of those whose crimes are proven. There can be no impunity for coup articulations nor tolerance for initiatives aimed at subverting the popular will expressed at the ballot box. The defense of democratic freedoms also requires confronting the economic and political forces that finance, sustain and seek to legitimize the far right in Brazil. The participation or facilitation of Javier Milei’s government in Flávio Bolsonaro’s movement through Argentine territory adds another worrying element to this scenario. The articulation between far-right governments, neofascist political forces and sectors of US imperialism constitutes a concrete threat to the sovereignty and democratic achievements of the Latin American peoples. This convergence is not limited to solidarity among reactionary leaders, but expresses an identity of economic and social projects: submission to international financial capital, privatization of national wealth, destruction of labor rights, repression of popular movements and deepening of economic dependence. It is a continental alliance of the dominant classes against the workers and peoples of the region, in which neofascism appears as a political instrument for preserving the privileges of big capital. The PCB warns that US imperialism will not remain passive in the face of the political defeats of its allies in Latin America. The crisis of US international hegemony, far from making its foreign policy less aggressive, tends to stimulate new forms of intervention, economic blackmail and political destabilization. In this scenario, the defense of national and popular sovereignty is indissolubly linked to internationalist solidarity with the peoples who resist imperialist domination, especially Cuba, Venezuela, Palestine and the other countries subjected to threats, blockades and aggressions. It is necessary to strengthen the sovereign integration of the Latin American peoples, combat the foreign military presence in the region and reject any attempt to turn our continent into a territory subordinate to Washington’s interests. Faced with this conjuncture, the Brazilian Communist Party calls on the working class, the youth, the popular movements and all democratic and anti-imperialist forces to maintain permanent mobilization against fascism, neoliberalism and foreign interference. The electoral defeat of Bolsonarism represented an important democratic conquest, but the political and social battle is far from over. We cannot allow imperialist interests to condition the future of Brazil or allow the popular victory to be emptied by the continuity of economic policies favorable to big capital. The struggle against neofascism also requires confronting neoliberalism, the concentration of wealth and the policy of class conciliation, which preserves the economic and political power of the dominant sectors responsible for sustaining the reaction. It is necessary to transform resistance against the maneuvers of imperialism into a powerful political and social offensive of the workers, strengthening their class organizations, preserving their political independence and expanding their capacity for mobilization and struggle. The defense of the legitimacy of the electoral result and of democratic freedoms must be articulated with the conquest of new rights, the revocation of neoliberal counter-reforms and the construction of a political alternative committed to the historical interests of the working class. Only the independent organization of the workers, popular mobilization and the struggle for people’s power will be able to confront the economic and social roots of fascism, break with imperialist domination and open the way for the construction of a sovereign, democratic and socialist Brazil. -Brazilian Communist Party Central Committee – National Political Commission The post The Flight of Flávio Bolsonaro and the Maneuvers of the Empire appeared first on MLToday .

articles.title: The Limits of Going it Alone: Lessons from Dan Osborn’s Defeat in Nebraska
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By Les Leopold November 4, 2026 lesleopold.substack.com Dan Osborn, the independent candidate and former local union president, once again came within a few percentage points of winning the Nebraska U.S. Senate seat. (He lost by 6.7% in 2024 and the same again this year.) He mounted an impressive challenge, but he couldn’t close the gap. Why? And what does his defeat tell us about the future of independent working-class politics? Wouldn’t Osborn have done much better if he ran as a Democrat? The anti-Trump Blue Wave created key red state Senate Democratic victories as it tore through Texas, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio, South Carolina, and maybe even Mississippi. But, it hit the shoals in North Dakota where the Democrat lost by 20.7 percent, by 18 percent in Oklahoma, and by 30.4 percent in Wyoming. The wave also didn’t reach the rest of the South and border states. So, it is not at all clear that a Democrat would have outperformed Osborn in Nebraska. Nevertheless, there are several lessons from Osborn’s defeat worth considering. 1. Running for the Senate is a big deal. Anyone running for the U.S. Senate against a Republican in a very red state is going to face a wall of money. There are only a handful of genuinely competitive Senate races every two years, and enormous sums flow into them. Osborn was up against $37 million—about $40 per voter— the most ever spent on a Senate race in Nebraska . It would be nice to think money doesn’t matter, but when the sums are that enormous it does. Money buys advertising, organization, visibility, and an increased ability to define a candidate, as well as to define the candidate’s opponent. Overcoming those advantages is extraordinarily difficult. 2. Running for the Senate is a big jump. I can’t think of anyone who has gone directly from serving as a local union president to being elected to the U.S. Senate. That’s a hell of a leap, and Osborn deserves enormous credit for attempting it. But it raises a question: Why not first run for a less demanding office, build an organization, establish a political record, and develop a broader base of support? Why not Congress or the state legislature? We can second guess all we want, but there’s no guarantee that a smaller race would have been easier for Osborn. And sometimes political opportunities don’t wait. Especially because building political power takes time, which means the odds were stacked against Osborn from the start. 3. Was he really an independent, or a Democrat in disguise? Everyone knows the Democratic brand is in terrible shape in Nebraska, as well as in much of red America. We did a survey that shows how much. Running as an independent, for Osborn, made considerable sense. But according to the New York Times , “more than half of voters — 55 percent — say they see Mr. Osborn, a union leader, as more of a Democrat than anything else. Just one third of voters say they consider him to be an independent.” And, of course, the Republicans spent millions hammering away at that perception throughout the campaign. To make matters worse, a leaked recordings captured Osborn privately expressing views that were far more liberal from the more cautious public positions he took during the campaign on issues like the border wall, transgender people, and ICE. Whether or not voters agreed with the positions on those issues he’d taken in public, the episode created a credibility problem. It reinforced the Republican argument that Osborn was really a Democrat hiding behind an independent label. This points to a larger problem: An independent candidate running alone must convince voters that his independence is real if he’s going to avoid negativity of the Democratic brand in red America. Share 4. There is no substitute for building an independent political organization, step by step. Osborn could be labeled—or mislabeled—a Democratic shill precisely because he was an individual candidate. He did not represent a political organization with a record of independence from the two major parties. He had no established movement behind him to demonstrate what that independence meant. As an individual, it was all on him. Compare that with the Nonpartisan League, which prospered in North Dakota during and after World War I. It had a coherent platform, including the public ownership of grain elevators and the establishment of a publicly owned bank. (The public Bank of North Dakota still operates today.) In a few years, the League recruited tens of thousands of dues-paying members and ran candidates for local and state offices. It was never about one person. It was a movement and a political organization. The verbal gaffes or vulnerabilities of any individual candidate could not bring down the entire effort. Building that kind of organization takes longer than trying to produce a dramatic political breakthrough from the top down. It’s not impossible for one individual to pull it off—Osborn has come remarkably close—but relying on one candidate makes the entire effort vulnerable to that person’s mistakes, inconsistencies, or political liabilities. (Consider the Dem’s experience with Graham Plattner in Maine.) An organization built around a clear platform is much stronger over the long run. It can explain, over several years and through many different candidates, what it means to be independent of the two major parties. Its record, membership, and collective work become the proof of its independence, and it becomes much more difficult to dismiss the entire organization as a Democratic front. 5. Osborn’s race shows why we need a long-term vision for a new working-class party. Or will the Democrats again become the party of working people? The alternative to running as an individual is the creation of a new political organization of working people—one that is fundamentally different from the Democrats and the Republicans. But why bother? Aren’t the Democrats now positioned to fight for powerful pro-worker policies like raising the minimum wage, facilitating labor union organizing, and putting price controls on pharmaceutical and food cartels? Let’s hope so. But, it’s just as possible for the Democrats with narrow victories in purple districts to call for moderate policies to secure their positions and maintain the support of their wealthy donors. Although we might see a slew of investigations to uncover corruption and the Epstein files, there may be little movement on the most basic economic protections for working people. And the Democrats still do not have the support of a majority of voters without college degrees, according to exit polls . Therefore, it would be prudent to lay the foundation for an independent party that would be overtly committed to take on corporate power, runaway inequality, and job insecurity. It would fight for good jobs, decent wages, strong unions, and support for communities where working people can thrive. But it would also have to welcome working people with a range of social and cultural beliefs, including people who might not feel comfortable with the progressive left. That doesn’t mean abandoning basic principles of fairness, equality, and justice. It does mean recognizing that working people will not agree on everything, and that a successful political organization must be broad enough to unite them around their common economic interests. Most important, it must be a party of and by working people . Its members—not wealthy donors, not political consultants, not a handful of prominent leaders—must shape its platform, choose its candidates, run its campaigns, and recruit new members. It must be an organization people actively participate in, not simply a label they vote for every few years. Dan Osborn’s campaign demonstrated that an independent working-class candidate could mount a serious challenge in a red state. His defeat should not obscure that achievement. But it also reminds us that even the strongest individual candidate cannot substitute for the patient work of building an independent political movement. We need to move beyond the search for the next Dan Osborn. We need to build a political organization that can produce hundreds of them. Let’s hope Osborn’s remarkable effort helps lay the foundation for that movement. The post The Limits of Going it Alone: Lessons from Dan Osborn’s Defeat in Nebraska appeared first on MLToday .

articles.title: Democrats, Please Take Note: Peace Is Good Politics
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By Jeffrey D. Sachs November 5, 2026 Commons Dream Voters across the United States were loud and clear on Tuesday in their historic drubbing of Trumpism . The election was a decisive rejection of Trump’s war on Iran and its staggering costs at home. While savoring their victory and the historic opportunity to restore America’s constitutional order, the Democrats should take the anti-war message of the election to heart, because they suffered the same verdict two years ago, when voters rejected the Biden administration’s wars in Ukraine and Gaza . Last week Israeli voters rejected Netanyahu’s reckless wars, and European voters are also rejecting parties that prolong the Ukraine War . The message of voters is the same everywhere: diplomacy is safer, more effective, and trillions of dollars cheaper than war. On election night Trump conceded to Fox News, “I think a part of it was Iran.” The next day Vice President JD Vance was far blunter, posting on X : “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night…. everyone knows why we lost.” In the AP Voter Poll, about 60 percent of voters said the decision to use military force against Iran was wrong , and about 90 percent called the cost of living a crucial or major factor in their vote . The war and the cost of living were of course utterly intertwined. Gasoline prices, around $2.80 per gallon before the war began on February 28, had risen by about 55 percent by mid-May and reached a monthly average of $4.43 in September . The 10-year Treasury yield climbed from below 4 percent before the war to above 5 percent in the autumn , and the Pentagon sought more than $200 billion in supplemental war funding . Every family with a mortgage, a car loan or a credit card balance suffered from the war. Voters everywhere are sending the same message: peace through diplomacy. The first duty of the new Congress is to restore its constitutional authority over war and its power of the purse to ensure that US forces are not sent back into combat in Iran or anywhere else on the whim of a president and the behest of domestic or foreign lobbies. Trump must of course refrain from restarting the war, which was never remotely necessary or justified. Remember that on February 28, the day the US and Israel launched the war, Oman’s foreign minister, who was mediating the U.S.-Iran talks, had said that a deal was within reach . The Democrats should not imagine that the anti-war lesson applies only to Republicans . Kamala Harris lost in 2024 because voters held the Biden administration responsible for the costs of its own wars. The energy shock that followed the escalation of the Ukraine war in 2022 drove up inflation , and gasoline topped $5 per gallon for the first time in June 2022 . Biden twice rejected negotiations that could have ended the conflict: in December 2021, when his administration refused to negotiate on NATO enlargement in response to Russia’s draft security treaty , and in April 2022, when the Istanbul talks were abandoned at the behest of the US and UK. The Gaza genocide also cost the Democrats directly. Among Americans who voted for Joe Biden in 2020 but not for Harris in 2024, 29 percent named ending Israel’s violence in Gaza as the main factor in their decision , the most frequently cited issue. The party’s voters have moved far ahead of its leaders. A New York Times/Siena poll in May 2026 found that roughly three-quarters of Democratic voters oppose US military and economic assistance to Israel . Voters everywhere are sending the same message: peace through diplomacy. On October 27, after Israeli wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, Netanyahu lost his majority . Similarly, European leaders who have tied themselves to open-ended war in Ukraine are being rejected by the voters. Only 10 percent of Germans are satisfied with Chancellor Friedrich Merz , the lowest rating ever recorded for a German chancellor. Emmanuel Macron’s approval fell to 15 percent in October . In Bulgaria, Iliana Iotova, who favors dialogue with Moscow , won the presidency on November 1 with more than 58 percent of the vote . A key upcoming key test for the Democrats will be Ukraine. They must stop their party’s typical Russia-bashing and instead support a diplomatic end to the war. As a start, the Democrats should remember why the war started. In 1990 the United States assured Mikhail Gorbachev that NATO would not move “one inch eastward.” The Clinton administration broke that promise. In 2008 the Bush administration pushed through the Bucharest declaration that Ukraine and Georgia “will become members of NATO,” despite Ambassador William Burns’s warning that this was the brightest of all red lines for Russia. In 2014 the United States backed the coup against Ukraine’s elected president, Viktor Yanukovych, as the leaked Nuland-Pyatt call made clear. In April 2022, when negotiators in Istanbul came close to a peace agreement based on Ukrainian neutrality, the US and UK actually intervened to block the agreement. Today 75 percent of Ukrainians support negotiations with Russia to end the war . The Democrats should not mistake their victory for a mandate to pursue their own wars. In view of these causes of the war, I have recently set out a straightforward diplomatic framework for peace in Ukraine that would end the war. NATO would end its eastward expansion. Ukraine would adopt permanent neutrality on the model of Austria in 1955 . An armistice line would be drawn, with both sides renouncing the use of force to change it. Ukraine would pursue membership in the European Union as a permanently neutral state. The Democrats should support such a diplomatic approach. It’s what can end the war, save Ukraine, and win the backing of both the Ukrainian and American people. Most importantly, the Democrats should not mistake their victory for a mandate to pursue their own wars. The new Democratic majority should quickly reassert the constitutional authority of Congress over war and peace, champion a negotiated peace in Ukraine, end support for Israel’s wars, cut the military budget , and redirect the savings toward lowering the cost of living and repairing the public finances. These positions are not only right but are good politics. For the Democrats to win the White House in 2028, they should become the party of peace. Better yet, both parties should become parties of peace and conduct the 2028 campaign on which party will best address America’s needs for decent jobs, affordability, healthcare , housing, a safe environment, and quality education.
