articles.title: Shenzhen’s nuclear summit
articles.author: Vijay Prashad
articles.content: On November 19, President Xi Jinping of China hosted a meeting with President Vladimir Putin of Russia and President Donald Trump of the United States. They met in Shenzhen at the margins of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum. The final statement that appeared from them had a very powerful line, “A nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.” This line came from three of the most important nuclear weapons countries in the world, only one of which – the United States – has used a nuclear bomb against civilians (in Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945). The other nuclear weapons countries (France, India, Israel, North Korea, Pakistan, and the United Kingdom) do not have the scale of the arsenals of the three that met in Shenzhen, which means that they do not have the capacity for a full nuclear war; for most of them, the nuclear weapons are a deterrent against the destruction of their state by others. The statement from these three powers, then, is indicative of the mood toward a new agreement on the danger and futility of nuclear weapons. The earliest treaty around the use of nuclear weapons was signed on December 1, 1959. This Antarctic Treaty banned nuclear explosions and radioactive waste disposal in Antarctica. It was followed on December 5, 1963 with the Partial Test Ban Treaty between the USSR, the United States, and the United Kingdom. This second treaty prohibited nuclear explosions in the atmosphere, in outer space, and underwater, while leaving underground testing permitted (this was eventually banned by the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test Ban Treaty of September 10, 1996, although the major nuclear powers have not signed onto it yet). Over the past sixty-seven years, we saw an increase in treaties to manage the diabolical presence of nuclear weapons for the first decades, and then we saw a collapse of the entire nuclear management machinery. That machinery has been dismantled piece by piece. The Shenzhen meeting is the first in very many years that revives the language of the danger of nuclear war and should be built upon by all peace-loving people. The collapse of nuclear weapons management On February 5, 2026, New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) expired. Signed in 2010 and extended in 2021, this treaty had restricted deployed US and Russian strategic nuclear forces and provided mechanisms for verification. It is the last of the treaties that manage the nuclear weapons arsenals of the nuclear weapons states to lapse. There are now no binding numerical limits on the nuclear weapons arsenals. Reacting to this, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said , “For the first time in more than half a century, we face a world without any binding limits on the strategic nuclear arsenals.” It would be inaccurate to say that no nuclear weapons agreements remain. The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty continues to exist, as do other nuclear treaties and obligations. The specific danger is that the two states possessing the largest arsenals (the USA and Russia) no longer operate under a binding bilateral ceiling on their strategic nuclear forces. Assurances of restraint cannot replace inspections, exchanges of information, agreed definitions, and enforceable limits. Political understandings can disappear with a change of government or a deterioration in relations. That is why the Shenzhen statement is significant, but only if it rebuilds a new treaty between these countries. The record of what has been lost is sobering: First. The Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) Treaty, signed in 1972, limited missile defense systems and helped to anchor the strategic relationship between Washington and Moscow. The United States withdrew on June 13, 2002, when US President George W. Bush decided to take advantage of temporary Russian weakness to advance the goals of US power. Whatever the limited promise made for missile defense, the abandonment of negotiated restraints encouraged adversaries to seek new means of overcoming those defenses. Military spending, a waste of social wealth, began to balloon upwards. Second. The Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, signed in 1987, eliminated US and Soviet ground-launched missiles with ranges between 500 and 5,500 kilometers. Washington withdrew from the treaty on August 2, 2019, when President Trump decided to press further US advantages against Russia. An entire category of weapons, once removed through negotiation, returned to military planning. This withdrawal further cornered Russia and provoked the invasion of eastern Ukraine. These two examples are the culmination of years of erosion across several areas of arms control. But they are the most significant treaties to have been set aside, and therefore put the world into a new arms race, particularly a new nuclear arms race. These agreements were a product of fear and political calculation. They were needed to understand that an adversary’s insecurity could become everyone’s catastrophe. In that sense, the inspections and the restrictions operated as confidence building measures across disagreements. Their destruction has restored a dangerous dependence on threat assessments, intelligence estimates, and the judgment of leaders operating under pressure. At Shenzhen, three leaders did not announce any reductions, verification arrangements, or timetable for negotiations, but they have established a political opening through which a peace agenda could be rebuilt. China’s participation adds an important dimension, since Beijing has not been a party to most of these bilateral treaties. A durable framework must address Beijing’s security concerns as well as those of Washington and Moscow. Humanity cannot afford to dismiss an opening for negotiation because it falls short of an agreement. Europe’s absence The absence of Europe at the meeting in Shenzhen is notable. Rather than accept the deescalation that could result from the meeting in China, the European leaders gathered in Berlin for a Coalition of the Willing meeting. This name, Coalition of the Willing, comes from a platform developed by retired UK politician Keir Starmer in March 2025, with the stated purpose for European leaders to support Ukraine’s military. If in Shenzhen the three major powers spoke of their concern for nuclear war and war in general, at Berlin the Europeans spoke of increased military expenditure, weapons deliveries, and an increased pressure campaign against Russia. Coalition members reaffirmed a pledge of €70 billion in military equipment, assistance, and training for Ukraine in 2026, with at least equivalent support in 2027. They proposed stronger economic pressure on Russia and discussed a European-led multinational force, supported by the United States, to operate after a ceasefire. These commitments extended the material infrastructure of confrontation. Shenzhen focused on de-escalation through engagement, while Berlin put the matter of escalation of military commitments firmly on the table. The European leaders’ talk of military expenditure came as their own populations took to the streets to condemn the austerity agenda that would make Europe more impoverished and more insecure. There was no public mention of these protests, nor was there acknowledgment that their agenda has very low public support . Opposition to the agenda of increased military spending and increased social austerity reaches 63% in Italy, 59% in Austria, 56% in Germany, and 55% in Estonia. The statement itself is anodyne, asking for greater military spending and for Russian concessions but it does not spell out a broad plan for European security. The entire agenda relies upon Europe’s dependency on Washington for crucial military capabilities and diplomatic access. This makes the Berlin agenda utterly unsustainable. BRICS+ agenda The opening of new negotiations for nuclear weapons control carries particular significance for the BRICS+ agenda. Countries outside the principal military blocs would bear devastating consequences from a confrontation they neither initiated nor controlled. Their interest in reducing nuclear danger is direct, which is why they should press for negotiations rather than leave the issue to an exclusive conversation among the largest powers. China and Russia attended Shenzhen in their national capacities. Their participation did not give them a mandate to bargain for the entire Global South. The test is whether their diplomacy creates greater room for other countries to pursue development, trade, and independent foreign policies. Reduced confrontation could open that space; an arrangement protecting only the privileges of powerful states would narrow its promise. BRICS+ has already connected disarmament to its practical development agenda. Resources consumed by arms races are unavailable for public health, housing, ecological repair, and productive investment. Its institutions can widen access to finance while its members demand that the nuclear powers fulfill their responsibilities. The New Development Bank’s pursuit of lending in members’ national currencies illustrates one avenue for increasing countries’ economic options. At the 19th BRICS+ Summit to be held in China, the issue of the trade-off between development and war will likely be further discussed. Shenzhen’s importance lies in the possibility it reopened. Three nuclear powers acknowledged a shared danger at a moment when binding restraints have disappeared. The task now is to make their acknowledgment material: negotiations, verification, limits, and reductions. Humanity needs an international movement strong enough to insist that the next announcement concerns weapons withdrawn and agreements signed, rather than another budget for preparing the war no society can survive. Vijay Prashad is an Indian historian and journalist. He is the author of forty books, including Washington Bullets, Red Star Over the Third World, The Darker Nations: A People’s History of the Third World, The Poorer Nations: A Possible History of the Global South, and How the International Monetary Fund Suffocates Africa, written with Grieve Chelwa. He is the executive director of Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research , the chief correspondent for Globetrotter, and an editor at LeftWord Books (New Delhi). He also appeared in the films Shadow World (2016) and Two Meetings (2017). This article was produced by Globetrotter and No Cold War .

articles.title: Belgium: 70,000-strong anti-austerity demonstration rounds up weekend of mobilization
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: A weekend of mobilization in Belgium culminated in a national anti-austerity demonstration in Brussels on Monday, November 23, with unions reporting at least 70,000 participants. After a successful youth strike against militarization and conscription on Friday and a peace march on Sunday, trade unions called on everyone to mobilize against the Arizona government’s devastating budgetary plans. Read more: One million students across Europe strike against war and rearmament “People are already struggling to make ends meet,” Peter Mertens , General Secretary of the Workers’ Party of Belgium (PTB-PVDA), wrote on the day. “They refuse to see billions poured into US-made F-35 fighter jets while we’re told there’s no money to invest in education or healthcare.” “And they refuse to accept that billionaires continue to get off the hook. That is why people are angry. And they have every reason to be.” A staged budgetary deadlock? Bart De Wever’s coalition is aiming to cut at least €10 billion from social security, including healthcare and pension rights, while planning to spend approximately €34 billion on rearmament by 2034. A massive mobilization wave broke out against these plans at the beginning of the government’s tenure and hasn’t stopped since. The pressure has succeeded in winning concessions. More recently, federal budget negotiations have also hit what seems a more substantial obstacle, as coalition partners continue to fail to reach an agreement. Weeks ago, Prime Minister De Wever even offered his resignation to the king – but was rejected . Progressive groups emphasized that De Wever had previously used a similar maneuver to pressure coalition members. And while there is no budgetary agreement yet, PTB-PVDA warns that things would not substantially change even if the social-democratic party Vooruit were to secure the concessions it is seeking. Throughout the weekend, protesters demanded and end to rising military expenses and more investments into social protection. Source: PTB-PVDA/Facebook “The governing parties already agree on most of the austerity package,” PTB-PVDA President Raoul Hedebouw commented last week. “Billions in cuts to healthcare, another attack on wage indexation, higher VAT.” “The real wrangling is over a few hundred million more or less for the so-called broadest shoulders,” he added. “Vooruit needs a symbolic gesture to sell this antisocial agreement. But De Wever refuses even that. The super-rich must be spared at all costs.” “The problem is not the share of the rich in a €10 billion austerity package, but the austerity package itself. Social alternatives to our budget exist. A genuine millionaire’s tax on net assets above €5 million would raise €8 billion a year. We can also phase out the billions in inefficient corporate subsidies and scale back the explosion in military spending.” Protests to break one of the EU’s great taboos The call to reject military investments at the expense of social justice spread throughout rallies over the weekend. On Saturday, approximately 5,000 people protested “to break one of the great taboos of the government and the European Union: spending billions on weapons and preparations for war at the expense of our future,” wrote PTB-PVDA’s Marc Botenga . Approximately 5,000 people marched against war and militarization on Sunday, November 22. Source: PTB-PVDA/Facebook “No,” echoed student organization Comac . “We refuse your billions for war and your cuts to education. We choose peace.”

articles.title: With the main opposition party suspended, Ecuador returns to the polls
articles.author: BreakThrough News
articles.content: On November 12, the campaigns for Ecuador’s local elections formally began. This Sunday, November 29, voters will elect prefects, mayors, city council members, and members of local boards. Historically, local elections have reflected the level of support or opposition to the current government. In this sense, right-wing president Daniel Noboa has more at stake than just a simple popular election. This is especially true when considering the last elections (which centered on four referendum questions) held on November 16, 2025. In those elections, Noboa suffered a fourfold electoral defeat, as the majority of Ecuadorians rejected his attempt to repeal the current constitution – which guarantees rights – in favor of a neoliberal one. Furthermore, Ecuadorians said no to the possibility of establishing foreign military bases. The defeat took the government by surprise, as it had been confident of a victory in a country that, in recent history, has consistently voted “yes” in referendums held by successive administrations. Read more: Ecuadorian people deal a crushing blow to neoliberalism in Noboa’s referendum And for that very reason, Noboa needs a victory at all costs. But it is important to understand that success for Noboa does not necessitate that his candidates win, but rather that his main opponent – Correísmo – loses. Noboa’s anti-Correa crusade From the very beginning, his main selling point (and the primary reason for the support that enabled him to win two presidential elections) has been to present himself as the antithesis of the supporters of Ecuador’s former president, the progressive Rafael Correa (2007–2017). As a result, Noboa has been viewed by many as a key player capable of preventing the return of Correísmo to the presidency, and it is precisely this antithetical distinction that keeps him a politically relevant figure. This has led Correa’s own party, the Citizen Revolution, to claim that the elections on November 29 will take place in an undemocratic and authoritarian environment, in which most institutions – including electoral ones – serve the interests of the executive branch. The main basis for this accusation stems from the suspension of the Citizen Revolution party in early 2025. The party’s candidates have been forced (when possible) to seek participation in the elections on other parties’ slates. Added to this is a series of allegations from the opposition regarding alleged political persecution against the main political leaders of the Citizen Revolution and their allies. Several months have already passed since Aquiles Álvarez, the then-mayor of Guayaquil, Ecuador’s largest city, was imprisoned in a maximum-security prison. The current mayor of Quito, the capital, Pabel Muñoz, who is seeking reelection, has been accused of various alleged crimes . The mayor of Cuenca was removed from office, and the prosecutor’s office is currently seeking to arrest him. Opposition leader Luisa González jailed by Noboa government One of the most emblematic cases is that of Luisa González, president of the Citizen Revolution and a two-time presidential candidate (who lost to Noboa both times). González was seeking the governorship of Manabí (a stronghold of Correísmo) but on October 22, she was arrested and has been held in prison on charges of money laundering ever since. Read more: Luisa González, former presidential candidate and opposition leader, is arrested in Ecuador And while the executive branch defends these actions by linking the Citizen Revolution to organized crime, the Correístas insist that this is political persecution, and that the upcoming election is one in which every effort has been made to ensure that their candidates fail to win elected office; therefore, they claim, the current government is seeking to ensure the victory of candidates close to it, who would run as candidates for other parties. Thus, according to this interpretation, Noboa seeks to win with his own candidates and with allied candidates from other parties. But his greatest victory would be to prevent the Citizen Revolution from achieving wins that would once again call into question his popularity, which has not recovered from its slight but steady decline over the past several months. For their part, the polls have once again shown clear inconsistencies among themselves, which has raised suspicions of alleged political manipulation of the numbers. In some polls, candidates opposed to the government hold a slight lead over many pro-government candidates or those allied with the executive branch. Other polls, however, show Noboa’s candidates in the lead. However, since these are regional elections, they will reveal different political realities and aspirations depending on the region under consideration. And while a country as complex and diverse as Ecuador may offer various paths forward, there are four provinces (Guayas, Pichincha, Manabí, and Azuay) and three cities (Quito, Guayaquil, and Cuenca) that will surely attract the most attention. They are home to a huge percentage of the population and tend to set the pace and political trends for the 2028 presidential elections.

articles.title: Morocco jails four Sahrawi students over political prisoner protest
articles.author: Pavan Kulkarni
articles.content: Condemning the sentencing of four Sahrawi students for taking part in a peaceful demonstration in solidarity with Sahrawi political prisoners, human rights groups in Western Sahara have called for greater international scrutiny of Morocco as an occupying power. The four jailed students are Brahim Babit, Salah Eddine Sbar, El Hussein Chihab, and Mohamed Lemrabet, studying at Zohr University in the Moroccan city of Agadir. On October 12, they traveled over 500 km north to the national capital, Rabat, to attend the demonstration. It was organized by family members and relatives of those incarcerated during the 2010 Gdeim Izik protest encampment for Sahrawi rights.​ Sahrawi students in Morocco report widespread discrimination, cultural pressure, and clashes over protests about the occupation of Western Sahara. The occupation curtails education. “There are no institutions of higher education in Western Sahara,” which forces students to go to Morocco to continue their studies, said Babouzeid Labbihi, executive member of the Collective of Sahrawi Human Rights Defenders in Western Sahara (CODESA).​ In the shadow of Gdeim Izik Gdeim Izik is a mostly uninhabited place in the Sahara Desert, about 15 km from Laayoune, the largest city in occupied Western Sahara. It entered the annals of history in 2010, when it became the site of a momentous mobilization widely described as a precursor to the Arab Spring. Protesting against discrimination by the occupation authorities, who prioritized Moroccan settlers for jobs, housing, education, and benefits, the Sahrawis, who were being pushed deeper into poverty, began pitching tents in Gdeim Izik on October 9, 2010. ​Within days, it grew into a mass protest encampment, with 20,000 protesters in 7,000 tents. Initially focused on socio-economic grievances, the demands grew bolder as the mobilization gathered momentum. Pro-independence slogans were raised against the occupation.​ On November 8, 2010, Moroccan military and police attacked the Gdeim Izik encampment. Protesters resisted. Hours of confrontation followed. ​ 700 Sahrawi civilians were wounded, 163 others went missing, and 36 people, including an eight-year-old, were killed, according to the Polisario Front (PF) , which the UN regards as the sole representative of the Sahrawi people. Morocco, however, admitted to only two civilian deaths, while claiming 11 of its security personnel were killed. Occupation forces detained up to 200, including women, children and the elderly. Based on confessions extracted under torture, the Moroccan military court sentenced 21 Sahrawis to prison terms ranging from 20 years to life. A subsequent re-trial by a civilian court in 2017 did little to alleviate their plight. Political prisoners on hunger strike Eight of them are serving life sentences , while 11 others are serving terms of between 20 and 30 years. For 16 years now, they have been enduring relentless and systematic harassment and mistreatment in Moroccan prisons, said Labbihi. On September 23, 2026, nine of these prisoners began a hunger strike.​ In solidarity with them, their family members and relatives called for a protest in Rabat on October 12, insisting that their internationally recognized rights as political prisoners be respected. Concerned about their deteriorating health, family members demanded independent medical care for the prisoners.​ They also called for the prisoners to be transferred to a facility in Laayoune, closer to their family, and demanded access to regular visits and phone calls.​ “Their very existence as Sahrawi political beings poses a threat to Moroccan colonization” Barely 40 protesters had gathered outside the Moroccan prison administration’s headquarters in Rabat when security forces surrounded them to prevent others from joining in. Unfazed, some protesters raised the Sahrawi flag and chanted slogans, calling for Sahrawi independence and freedom for all political prisoners. Allegedly assaulting the protesters, the security forces detained seven of them. Sahrawi human rights defenders Hassan Douihi, Khalid Boufrayout, and Aziz El-Wahidi were released without prosecution. The four students from Zohr University in Agadir – Babit, Sbar, Chihab, and Lemrabet – were put on trial, which was finally held on November 13 after two postponements . ​ Human rights defenders and Sahrawi students, along with Ruth Sebastián García and María Dolores Travieso – Spanish observers from the International Association of Jurists for Western Sahara – were barred from attending the trial.​ The court of first instance sentenced the four students to two years in prison. Two of them – Babit and Sbar – had already served prison terms previously. In addition, the court also imposed a 15,000 Dirham fine on each. This fine, amounting to over $1,500, is a “financial catastrophe far exceeding the penalty of deprivation of liberty,” in Western Sahara, where most families struggle to get by, explained Labbihi. “Its aim is economic deterrence: to starve the activist’s family so that it pressures him to abandon the struggle. It is a collective punishment,” he said. “The Sahrawi students are not tried because they raised a flag, but because their very existence as Sahrawi political beings poses a threat to Moroccan colonization.” ​Moroccan occupation of Western Sahara With US support, Morocco illegally occupied Western Sahara – a northwest African country on the Atlantic coast, rich in phosphate and fisheries – in 1975, soon after the International Court of Justice (ICJ) dismissed Moroccan claims to sovereignty over the neighboring country. ​ In the over half a century since, the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU), the United Kingdom High Court of Justice (UKHCJ) and the African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights (AfCHPR) have all held that Morocco has no sovereignty over Western Sahara.​ The African Union (AU) also recognizes Western Sahara as a member state under occupation, while the UN lists it among the countries yet to be decolonized. However, with the backing of the US and its European allies, the Moroccan occupation continues into its 52nd year.​ ​

articles.title: One million students across Europe strike against war and rearmament
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: More than 50 student organizations in 27 European countries launched an international strike against war and militarization on Friday, November 20, drawing a million of young people onto the streets. Students issued joint demands including an end to rearmament and all forms of conscription, investment in education and social services, and solidarity with oppressed peoples around the world. They also declared resistance to growing authoritarian trends in the region. “We are protesting to claim our right to a better future, and we are aware that if we stand united, no one will be able to stop us from taking it,” said Alessandro Di Miceli from the Italian organization Rete della Conoscenza. The international student strike drew a million students onto the streets of 27 European countries on November 20, 2026. Source: BreakThrough News Actions took place in Norway, Sweden, Finland, Poland, Romania, Turkey, Greece, Croatia, Hungary, Slovakia, Austria, the Czech Republic, Germany, Denmark, the Netherlands, Belgium, Ireland, Italy, Britain, France, Switzerland, Spain, Portugal, Malta, and Slovenia, among others. “From the right to education to the right to housing, from the struggle against the rising costs of living and the climate crisis to the fight against militarization and rearmament, specific demands may differ from country to country, but are all deeply connected between each other,” Di Miceli said. Attacks on education funding One concern shared by student groups across the region is the precarious state of public education. For almost two months, high school and university students in France have led massive protests and occupations against austerity measures imposed during Emmanuel Macron’s presidency. Read more: 1.6 million join general strike in France against austerity Similar policies took root elsewhere too. In Britain, Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s administration recently announced cuts to student welfare and support while planning to invest billions in the military. “While the government says it doesn’t have the money to invest in education or opportunities for young people without cutting welfare and potentially pushing hundreds of thousands of young people into poverty, it is right now spending an extra £15 billion a year on the military,” Stop the War’s Shabbir Lakha wrote. Teachers and parents protested side by side with youth organizations in many cities supporting their concerns. Still in England, the National Education Union (NEU) published a statement on planned school funding cuts on the day of the international youth strike. The union found that mainstream school funding in England will be slashed by £1.2 billion (USD 1.57 billion) in cash in 2027-28. The cuts will affect approximately 11,000 schools in England, the NEU pointed out – many of them in the poorest parts of the country, including Hackney, Southwark and Tower Hamlets in London. “Hackney and Tower Hamlets have the highest child poverty rates in the UK: half of their children live in poverty once housing costs are paid,” NEU general secretary Daniel Kebede warned. Students refuse return of conscription Another concern widely voiced among student groups is the return of military conscription. In Germany , more than 50,000 pupils and students organized their fifth school strike in a year. The German government plans to build Europe’s “strongest conventional army” in a matter of years, while slashing welfare and social security – with the youth insisting they will not be part of this scenario. Similarly, in Belgium – including in Ghent, Brussels, Leuven, Liège, and Antwerp – young people tore up letters issued by the Ministry of Defense regarding military service. Read more: Gen Z protests in Germany met with racial profiling and police harassment In Slovenia , the Rosa Collective described how thousands of students attended a recent arms fair as part of their “active citizenship” curriculum while structural needs remain unaddressed. “The military is targeting rural vocational and technical high schools,” the group wrote. “They aim to recruit young people from socially disadvantaged backgrounds, offering them money and adventure.” Noting that Israeli arms companies Rafael and Israel Aerospace Industries appeared basically next door to the location visited by students, Rosa Collective warned that “young people are being recruited in secondary and primary (!) schools while some faculties and institutes are becoming incubators for the development of technologies for military use.” Convergence with housing and cost-of-living campaigns In Italy, Spain, and Portugal, the student strikes echoed mass mobilizations for housing and general strikes against the cost-of-living crisis. A national strike called by the mainstream trade union confederation CGIL was ongoing as students took to the streets in Italy, with progressive student collectives calling on the public to embrace a more ambitious agenda and support new mobilizations by grassroots unions on December 12 . In Spain, protesters cited the November 11 general strike as an inspiration. “We had an amazing strike last November 11, with more than 400,000 people marching only in Barcelona,” a spokesperson for Sindicat d’Estudiants told BreakThrough News . “And we said that day that this was not the ending of anything. We said that the demonstrations, that the strike had to keep going. And this is what we are doing today.” Students rejected war, rearmament, and the far right. Source: BreakThrough News “We are determined to continue organizing and mobilizing in the months ahead, until these demands become reality,” Shabbir Lakha emphasized in a statement by the Youth Strike Coalition. “The ruling classes of our countries should begin to worry, because this November 20 will only be the beginning. We will keep standing together as youth to fight for our future, not their wars.”

articles.title: “A Shameful Failure”: U.N. Climate Summit Collapses as Final Text Drops Mention of Fossil Fuels
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report . I’m Amy Goodman, back in New York. In Turkey, the United Nations climate summit collapsed Sunday after nations failed to reach an agreement on a new climate deal as the Earth warms. The European Union and a number of countries opposed the final draft because it made no mention of fossil fuels. The effort to strip the text of references to coal, oil and gas was led by Saudi Arabia and joined by Russia. The United States did not participate in COP31. This is Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, the climate envoy for the Marshall Islands. KATHY JETN̄IL- KIJINER : The Republic of the Marshall Islands objects to the adoption of the CMA text and cannot join consensus. We came to Antalya to honor our commitment to the Paris Agreement and to do what we promised our people back home. We face an inevitable overshoot of 1.5. We came here expecting the world to deliver a comprehensive and urgent response on reducing emissions, on protecting our people and on providing the finance to do this. We have been let down on all sides. We were presented with the worst possible response to overshoot: a response to enhance oil and gas. We will not be forced to accept false solutions. We will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests. We will not accept an outcome that undermines our security and threatens our future. AMY GOODMAN : Ireland’s Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien outlined the European Union’s opposition to the final text. DARRAGH O’BRIEN: At a point where the world urgently needs action to avert disastrous levels of global warming, the draft cover decision falls well short. We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science, that disregards the implementation gap, and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required to correct the overshoot and bring 1.5 degrees back to within reach. We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change. And we will not accept negotiating backward in time. And we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel. AMY GOODMAN : Over the weekend, climate justice activists rallied against the final text. On Friday, a Malaysian climate activist, Amalen Sathananthar, was detained after interrupting the closing plenary. He stood on a table holding a red noose around his neck and wearing a shirt that read, “You are killing the future.” AMALEN SATHANANTHAR : You are killing the future! You are killing the future! Why don’t you just kill me now? The climate crisis is killing! … There’s no money! Just kill me now! The Global South can’t wait! The Global South can’t wait for this! And yet you just keep doing nothing, nothing at all! Racists! Kill me now! Kill me now! Kill me now! Kill me now! … You are killing the future! You are killing the future! You are killing the future! You are killing the future! AMY GOODMAN : We are joined now by three leading climate justice activists who just returned to their home countries after attending the U.N. climate summit. Brandon Wu is with us from Washington, D.C., director of policy and campaigns at ActionAid USA . In Manila, Lidy Nacpil is with us, the longtime Filipina climate activist and coordinator with the Asian Peoples’ Movement on Debt and Development. And from Cape Town, South Africa, we’re joined by Tasneem Essop, executive director of the Climate Action Network International. I want to begin with Tasneem, but first let’s play a short video from Turkey of Tasneem Essop trying to interact with Chris Bowen, the COP31 president of negotiations from Australia. TASNEEM ESSOP : You have an opportunity to save this process. We need decisions that will protect the people of the South. There’s nothing in the text, and corporate interests will be the only ones that benefit. CCUS , carbon dioxide removals are dangerous, dangerous, opens the door for fossil fuels. Please read the letter. CHRIS BOWEN : I will. TASNEEM ESSOP : The Global South demands the protection of its people. AMY GOODMAN : “The Global South demands the protection of its people,” Tasneem Essop said, executive director of the Climate Action Network International, joining us from Cape Town, South Africa. Tasneem, you must be extremely tired at this point. I just saw you in Antalya, Turkey, and now you’re back home in Cape Town, South Africa. Can you respond to the collapse of the talks, as you tried to question the president of the COP , the Australian Climate Minister Chris Bowen? TASNEEM ESSOP : Thanks, Amy. Yeah, a bit tired from the COP itself, but also, in a sense, very disappointed that it had to come to this. I wouldn’t characterize the COP as having collapsed. I think it’s important for your viewers to understand that there were two processes, actually, at this COP . The one was the formal negotiation process, and that is where the negotiations on different tracks — on the just transition, on adaptation, on mitigation, on climate finance — was taking place. And then there was the cover decision. The cover decision was a decision by the COP presidencies, in fact, driven by the COP president for negotiations, Australia, as a way of including political statements, if I can call it that. And it’s really that where there was no agreement reached. The others had — you know, they were largely procedural. They had passed through. There was one or two where there were objections, like the mitigation work program track. But certainly, it was the cover decision that caused the most controversy. Presidencies do not need to have cover decisions. We were concerned about this cover decision from the start, when they announced this at the pre- COP . And so, we saw that, in fact, this cover decision distracted the entire negotiations. All of the political attention that was needed in the formal negotiations got taken out and into the cover decision negotiations and discussions. So, that is where things collapsed, if you might call it that. It’s disappointing that it had to come. I think the biggest lesson here is cover decisions just do not work. We need to pay attention and focus on the mandated negotiations. And that is where developed countries, actually, the ones that, you know, had the theater around rejecting a cover decision — that’s where they actually gutted the negotiations. That’s where — and it’s hidden — where the problems arose. The finance for adaptation track didn’t move forward. They kept on resisting the delivery plan for a commitment they made on tripling finance for adaptation. The just transition track didn’t move, because they obstructed the creation of a just transition mechanism. And so, if you go through all of the formal negotiation tracks, it was developed countries that actually blocked and obstructed, and then came to the cover decision and, you know, decided that they’re going to reject it, and pretended to be the champions, when, in fact, the real negotiations were happening elsewhere, and they actually obstructed this. AMY GOODMAN : I want to bring Brandon Wu into the conversation, of ActionAid USA . He also just returned from the U.N. climate summit. If you can give your analysis of what took place? A lot of people are saying COP31 collapses as EU rejects texts for being weak on fossil fuels. But when we were at the U.N. climate summit, we were speaking to many, including a young European activist who was saying, in fact, to their shock, the European Union replaced President Trump, who had pulled the U.S. out, in pushing for fossil fuels at the U.N. climate summit. What happened? BRANDON WU: So, I think this has become the headline. I mean, you read these headlines at the top of the show, right? The COP collapses, and it’s because — and the EU is rejecting the text because of lack of fossil fuels. And I do think that that is actually a dangerous and deeply misleading story, because, as Tasneem said, the EU, you know, try to style themselves as the climate champions: “This is not enough ambition. We need more movement on phasing out fossil fuels,” which, of course, we do. We need more movement on fossil — on phasing out fossil fuels. And it’s got to start in the Global North. The EU are being quite hypocritical, actually. Their transition plans away from fossil fuels are not at all aligned with the 1.5 degrees Celsius climate target that they claim to be defending so much. And the way these negotiations are structured, the Global North has the responsibility to reduce its emissions first and fastest, and also the responsibility to provide money and support to the Global South, so that the transition can be enabled in those poorer countries. And what we saw is that the developed countries, across the board, acted more like bullies than champions. They come in demanding more of the Global South, but in every negotiating room blocking any progress on the finance that is going to make that transition possible. And one thing, like two weeks before the negotiations started, the EU climate commissioner actually said any new climate finance commitments were, quote, “dead in the water.” “Dead in the water.” He actually said that. This was two months after the floods in Nepal that killed 1,500 people, with five over 5,000 people still missing. “Dead in the water.” It was shockingly tasteless and also a shocking way to approach the negotiations. They said out loud two weeks before the negotiations that they were coming in with nothing to offer, with no room for compromise on the one thing that is the major priority for the Global South countries in these negotiations. AMY GOODMAN : So, talk about what this means. What does it mean for the COP , for the conference of the parties, COP31, the longest, the largest, to collapse? And while I think up to 100,000 people participated, would you also say it’s one of the largest gatherings of fossil fuel lobbyists in the world? BRANDON WU: So, yes, there are a lot of fossil fuel lobbyists that come up into these spaces. There are a lot of lobbyists for data centers, for, you know, Big Tech, all these things. It’s not a clean space, right? And the reason we have so many intransigent governments is because there’s so many profit-seeking interests that have their ear. The way forward — I mean, as Tasneem said, the actual negotiations did not fully collapse. There were decisions that moved forward some key things on just transition, which is, you know, making sure communities are supported as we change our economies to more sustainable ones, on finance, on adaptation. Those tracks are not dead. We didn’t get anything we wanted, but it was only the cover decision that was fully rejected. And so we live to fight another day, but we’re going to face the same problem over and over again. This has been happening for decades, right? The way that these negotiations are structured is the Global North, as I said, has to lead, on cutting emissions, on providing finance. They have the legal obligation to do that. They have the money to do that. We see how the U.S. is throwing trillions of dollars a year for genocide and war. The money is there. They need to provide it to the Global South to make the transition happen, and then the Global South can reduce emissions, their dependence on fossil fuels. And what we’ve seen over the past decades is the Global North are not delivering on any of their responsibilities. That’s what’s causing the deadlock. It’s not new to this COP , but it’s becoming increasingly untenable. AMY GOODMAN : And, I mean, I think part of the problem, being at the COP for this past week, is the level of jargon that most people just don’t have access to — “adaptation,” “mitigation,” “climate finance.” These may sound obvious to you. The cover decision and the cover letter, explain exactly what you mean. BRANDON WU: Look, at the end of the day, this is a question of fairness. There are basic principles of fairness, that everyone understands, that are just being blown out of the water in this process. The rich developed countries — the U.S., EU, Australia, Japan, Canada — these are the countries that spewed greenhouse gases into the atmosphere over the last 150, 200 years, and have built their economies on the backs of fossil fuels. These are the countries that created the mess, and these are the countries that have to clean it up. “Climate finance” is just a fancy term for sending money to poorer countries so that they can make the transition, as well, so that they can help their communities survive in a world in which, you know, we’re breaching the 1.5-degree limit. That’s another piece of jargon, but what that means, of course, is that climate impacts are getting worse. We all know this. They’re getting worse. They’re going to get much worse, much faster, I think. And countries need the support to deal with that. These are countries that have had nothing to do with the problem, and it’s their people whose lives are at stake. They’re basic principles of fairness. I think everybody can understand that. AMY GOODMAN : And the cover decision? BRANDON WU: So, the cover decision, I mean, the reason that that’s important is because the rich countries are using what happened with the cover decision as a way to deflect blame. So, they are pointing at — AMY GOODMAN : And “cover decision” means? BRANDON WU: So, the cover decision, again, it was a political text, that came out of nowhere. The presidency of the COP wrote it, so Türkiye and Australia. It was not part of the formal negotiating tracks, where you have all the different country blocs talking about issues of substance that they’ve decided should formally be on the agenda for the negotiations. So, it’s a political text that was written by the presidency, and then they tried to, in a top-down way, get buy-in from all the countries so they could include all their little pet projects and all the pet projects of the countries that had their ear. AMY GOODMAN : I want to bring Lidy Nacpil into this conversation. Lidy Nacpil is a Filipina climate activist, coordinator with the Asian Peoples’ Movement on Debt and Development, with the Global Campaign to Demand Climate Justice. Lidy, thanks so much for being with us. You’re joining us, I believe, from Manila. Can you respond to what has taken place? You know, for so many COPs, so many of these U.N. climate summits, in the midst of them, the Philippines is hit with tsunamis, with hurricanes. I think of how many times Yeb Saño, first as a chief climate negotiator for the Philippines, now, as he’s described, as a climate pilgrim, but then he would stand up and talk about how the Philippines was being ravaged by the climate crisis. What this means for the Philippines, and what you think needs to happen now, Lidy? LIDY NACPIL : Well, first of all, our reaction to COP31 is also amidst the backdrop of the UNEP report saying that the breach of 1.5 degrees is imminent and unavoidable. So we thought that this would at least imbue a sense of urgency for this COP to deliver very concrete and actionable agreements that will actually mean progress in the real world and not just in text language. So, of course, we are so deeply disappointed and enraged that we have not made this progress, and, in fact, backtracked on a number of things. There are, of course, some important gains we have made in terms of securing at least some meager progress on certain things. Tasneem has mentioned, for instance, other negotiating tracks. But this is not what — the progress we needed at this point. We need much, much more. And in terms of the climate finance that we’re discussing here, I’d like to really make it clear: This is not about the Global South begging for assistance and help. And this is one of the worst things that happen at COPs. They make us feel like, OK, here we come again with our finance demands. But this is a matter of principle, as well as practicality. The principle is that they have created this problem, and they have to contribute to the solutions, including that of providing climate finance as part of the reparations for all the harm that has been caused. And the practicality is that we cannot fully transition away from fossil fuels, which we want to do. We will be one of the first people to be — to want to do that, because the impacts on us are huge and horrifying. But this is not simply possible to succeed in completing that transition if that climate finance is not delivered. And this is a fact that they continuously leave out in their stories. And when I say “they” here, it’s the Global North. The EU, for instance, we were very appalled that they were, as Brandon said, hypocritically saying they’re going to reject the cover decision because there’s no mention of fossil fuel transition, but they leave out the fact that this is not going to happen unless they deliver on their climate finance, which they have successfully obstructed in all the negotiation tracks, any discussion on finance. So, this leaves the Global South in a situation where we realize it’s — we really need to fight harder and build our power, because no way are these countries going to, or these governments, are going to negotiate it on the basis — negotiate on the basis of good faith, of good intention for the whole of humanity. And by the way, it is not just for our sake that we need to complete that transition in our countries for which we need the climate finance. It’s for the entire world’s sake. We’re not going to succeed in solving the climate problem with just actions in the Global North. We know that. We need to act in the Global South, but we need to do more than our fair share. And for that to happen, we definitely need that climate finance. So, we’re not here to beg. We are here to insist on what is owed us and to insist on what success for the whole of humanity, for the whole of the planet, what success requires. AMY GOODMAN : I want to bring in Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner. We’ve just spoken with three well-known activists who have attended so many of the climate summits, from the Philippines, from South Africa, from the United States. Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner is also an activist, but now the climate envoy, one of the delegates, the climate envoy for the Marshall Islands. We just played a clip of you speaking. And I wanted to ask you: What was it like from the inside? And how does climate change affect the Marshall Islands, even where they are? KATHY JETN̄IL- KIJINER : Yeah. Thank you, Amy. I’m so glad to be here, and I’m glad you were able to catch me, actually. But I would just say that in the — it was incredibly long hours of negotiations. I mean, I didn’t sleep that whole night. I got there to swap out my minister at 7 p.m., and then I was there until we delivered our statement. And so, we were negotiating at 3:00 in the morning, at 1:00 in the morning, and then again at 5:00 in the morning. And it was long hours of discussions between ourselves, our allies within the Pacific Small Island Developing States, within the Alliance of Small Island Developing States, and, of course, other countries, too. And we were really trying to figure out how do we make our way forward and whether or not we needed to sign on to the cover decision or not sign on to the cover decision. So, it was not an easy decision at all. But I think, ultimately, for us, this deal did not provide on fossil fuel transition that we needed. It did not have the ambition on finance, on adaptation finance. It did not have enough strong language on the ICJ . It did not recognize how incredibly monumental the ICJ was, especially for those of us in the Pacific. And then, of course, it did not have enough on any of the other components that were so important to us, on IPCC . And so, I think, ultimately, we did decide that we needed to not sign on to the cover decision. It is the first time that Marshall Islands did that, and we did not come to that decision lightly. But I think that I stand by it, you know, and I think that it was the right call to make. I think that the two COP presidencies had an incredibly difficult task of, first of all, working together, but also working with multiple different countries and all the different priorities. But I think the biggest thing of all was that we could not sign on to a decision that had to do with CCUS , the carbon capture, utilization, storage. We did not want this COP to be a CCUS . And, of course, I think also — AMY GOODMAN : Kathy, if you could explain what CCUS is, what these options are that are being talked about? KATHY JETN̄IL- KIJINER : Yeah. So, I’m not a climate scientist, so I’ll just say that CCUS is actually a way to capture carbon that actually utilizes fossil fuels. So, it basically would have opened up the way for more fossil fuel usage. And ultimately, we as the Marshall Islands could not agree to a deal that would actually open the path for further fossil fuel usage and actually make the environment worse. So, that was part of the reason why we didn’t sign on. But it was also because there was extremely weak language on adaptation finance. So, I think that’s really important, because I think what’s coming away is that a lot of countries are saying, “They walked away only because it did not have transition away from fossil fuels.” Yes, definitely, so important, and also it did not have enough on adaptation finance. Countries like mine need both. We cannot survive the climate crisis without the transition away from fossil fuels and without the needed adaptation finance for developing countries, that we’re duly owed. You know, the Marshall Islands is only two meters above sea level. We are dealing with massive impacts from climate, from climate change, including the worst drought in El Niño, super El Niño that’s about to hit us. And then we’re looking at adaptation at such a large scale, changing the landscape of our islands, that would cost tens of billions of dollars just for two of our urban centers. And we did not cause this problem. So, of course, we are owed that finance. So, I think that’s really important to come away with, too, is that we were betrayed on two fronts: on the transition away from fossil fuels and on adaptation finance. AMY GOODMAN : I just have to quickly ask: You are — there’s something oddly appropriate about you — I don’t think you’re in your closet. I think you’re in some kind of store. But there are pocket books everywhere, which suggest money. And maybe that’s the most appropriate way to understand what took place. KATHY JETN̄IL- KIJINER : Yes, yeah. You caught me on my day off right after, and so I’m out actually doing a little bit of sightseeing in Antalya. AMY GOODMAN : Amazing. I wanted to end back with Brandon Wu. You’ve returned to the United States. President Trump just had his trilateral summit, or, I should say, photograph, with President Xi of China and President Putin of Russia. And one of the deals in their so-called peace declaration was increasing the production of fossil fuels. If you can talk about what it means to come back to the historically largest emitter of carbon, of carbon pollutants in the world, after Trump just met with now the current largest producer of carbon pollutants in the world, China, and their resolution to increase oil, gas production? BRANDON WU: Yeah, I want to say two things about that. Excuse me. First, the U.S. is actually the country with the largest oil and gas expansion plans of any country in the world. And so, if we want to point a finger at anybody, it should be our own country, you know, and, of course, in addition to being the largest historical polluter. The second thing is that, you know, I think what this really shows is it actually comes back to the importance of a multilateral democratic process like the COPs. You know, we come away from these COPs every year saying, “Well, that was a disaster.” And then, of course, so we always ask ourselves, “What’s the point? Why are we still fighting in these places that are dominated by countries in the Global North that don’t want to do anything, that have fossil fuel lobbyists roaming the hallways? Like, why are we here? What are we accomplishing?” And I think that trilateral summit really shows us kind of what the alternative is. Right? It is a world that is dominated by autocrats, or wannabe autocrats, and strongmen, who have very little accountability. And that is what we’re up against, right? And the UNFCCC and the U.N. spaces, in general, provide an alternative to that, where everybody, at least in theory, formally has a voice, and we, as civil society, have a space to input and to protest and to advocate. And we have to preserve that. It’s not delivering the results that we need so far, and we know why. It’s because of the intransigence of many countries, where, as Lidy said, we need to be building power. We need to be pushing these governments to do better. Certainly in the U.S., we need to be doing that. And hopefully, we’ll have that opportunity in the very near future. But, yeah, I think the alternative to these multilateral spaces are places where we have even less power, even less of a say, and have even less of an opportunity to hold leaders accountable. AMY GOODMAN : Brandan Wu, director of policy and campaigns at ActionAid USA ; Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, climate envoy for the Marshall Islands; Tasneem Essop, executive director of the Climate Action Network International, speaking to us from Cape Town, South Africa; Lidy Nacpil, coordinator with the Asian Peoples’ Movement on Debt and development, speaking to us from the Philippines. We want to thank you all for being with us. Coming up, as Democrats flip another House seat in North Carolina, we speak to Bishop William Barber. He’s calling for the Third Reconstruction. What does that mean? What is he calling on Democrats to do, who now have the largest majority in the House of Representatives in 30 years? Stay with us. [break] AMY GOODMAN : “Fenfo,” “Something to Say,” by the Malian singer Fatoumata Diawara, performing in our Democracy Now! studio in 2018.

articles.title: We Need a Third Reconstruction: Bishop William Barber Pushes Democrats to Take Action After Midterms
articles.content: With Democrats preparing to take control of both houses of Congress in January, Bishop William Barber of Repairers of the Breach argues the coalition that delivered the Democrats their midterm victories must now hold the incoming Congress accountable and keep organizing from the ground up. He and other faith leaders are calling on members of the incoming Congress to join them outside the U.S. Capitol next month to sign “A Pledge for Moral Defiance” — a commitment to pass legislation that addresses the needs of poor and working people and other vulnerable communities. Barber is pushing for what he describes as a Third Reconstruction: a sweeping moral and political agenda that includes a living wage, universal healthcare, protecting voting rights, affordable housing, environmental justice and comprehensive immigration reform. “This was a vote not for Democrats,” says Barber. “It was a vote to say, 'Will you use policy to answer the pain that we are experiencing in this country at this particular moment?'”

articles.title: Francophonie Summit marked by absence of Sahel countries and DRC-Rwanda tensions
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: The 20th Francophonie Summit – the highest meeting of the International Organization of La Francophonie (OIF) – took place on November 14 – 16 in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, without three West African countries that have increasingly distanced themselves from France and its political influence in the region. The three-day summit, hosted for the first time by Cambodia, brought together leaders and representatives of French-speaking countries under the theme “Reinvesting in Peace for Shared Prosperity and Lasting Stability.” Among those attending was French President Emmanuel Macron, Rwandan President Paul Kagame, Democratic Republic of Congo President Félix Tshisekedi, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Vietnamese President To Lam, and Togolese President Faure Gnassingbé. However, the absence of the three Sahelian countries, alongside a bitter diplomatic dispute between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), continue to make the headlines. The Sahel’s departure from the Francophonie Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger were suspended from the OIF following military coups in 2020, 2022, and 2023, respectively. Their governments subsequently moved to end longstanding military and diplomatic arrangements with France, including the expulsion of French troops from their territories. In March 2025 , the three countries announced their withdrawal from the International Francophonie Organization (OIF). Niger and Burkina Faso communicated their decisions on March 17, followed by Mali on March 18, shortly before International Francophonie Day on March 20. In a joint communiqué, the foreign ministers of the three countries recalled their historical involvement in the organization, noting that they had participated as founding members in the 1970 Niamey Summit, which established the Agency for Cultural and Technical Cooperation (ACCT), the institution that eventually became the OIF. However, they accused the organization of abandoning its founding principles of cooperation, solidarity, and respect for cultural diversity following the military transitions in the three countries. Instead of supporting their populations’ aspirations, the OIF had distinguished itself through the “selective application of sanctions on the basis of geopolitical considerations and contempt for their sovereignty.” The ministers further accused the organization of becoming a “remotely controlled political instrument,” arguing that its actions contradicted its stated objectives of promoting peace, cooperation, and solidarity among member states. The communiqué stated that the three heads of state, Burkina Faso’s Captain Ibrahim Traoré, Mali’s General Assimi Goïta, and Niger’s Brigadier General Abdourahamane Tiani, had decided to withdraw their countries “in full sovereignty,” adding that the decision reflected their commitment to “defend their legitimate interests.” The departure carried a particular historical note. Mali and Niger were among the organization’s founding members, and the agreement establishing the ACCT was signed in Niamey on March 20, 1970. Their withdrawal, alongside Burkina Faso’s, was a major break with an institution that has historically connected France with countries across Africa and other parts of the world. Often described as the French-speaking equivalent of the Commonwealth, the OIF brings together 90 states and governments, comprising 53 full members, five associate members, and 32 observers. Leadership dispute exposes divisions between Rwanda and DR Congo The summit’s other major challenge was the failure to elect a secretary-general for the 2027–2030 term, following a diplomatic confrontation between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Rwanda’s Louise Mushikiwabo was seeking a third term, but her candidacy faced opposition from Congo, which accused Rwanda of supporting the M23 armed group operating in eastern DRC. The Congolese government had initially presented Juliana Lumumba as its candidate but subsequently withdrew her candidacy and backed Romania’s Dacian Cioloș. Mauritania’s Coumba Ba was also in the running. The dispute escalated when the DRC threatened to walk away . Rwanda, meanwhile, denounced France for interfering in the election after reports emerged that Macron had asked Kagame to withdraw Mushikiwabo’s candidacy, a request Rwanda rejected. Following closed-door negotiations, member states failed to reach a consensus. Instead, they agreed to extend Mushikiwabo’s mandate by 12 months and postpone the election until further notice. Despite the leadership impasse, the summit adopted three documents: the Phnom Penh Declaration, a resolution on crises and peacebuilding, and the Phnom Penh Appeal on protecting cultural heritage. France searches for new partnerships beyond the Sahel The summit took place amid France’s declining influence in parts of West and Central Africa, particularly following the withdrawal of its military presence from Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger. Macron’s attendance also came as he faces domestic political challenges, including protests over the cost of living, wages, inequality, and public services. The demonstrations have added pressure on the French government as the country approaches its next presidential election. Beyond the Sahel, France has increasingly sought to reposition its diplomatic and economic relations with other African countries. In May 2026, Macron co-hosted the Africa Forward Summit in Nairobi with Kenyan President William Ruto, the first in an English-speaking country. Progressives in Kenya argued that the Nairobi summit was an attempt by France to reposition itself, with East Africa emerging as a new strategic frontier. Read more: After setbacks in West Africa, France courts Anglophone Africa Francophonie as a political camp has challenges. Its members share a language, but not interests. Three founding members have walked out, the largest African member threatened to follow, and the leadership is deadlocked. The revival of France’s place in Africa and in a shifting world order is facing difficulties.

articles.title: Ansar Allah advances towards Saudi stronghold Aden
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: As the renewed fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Ansar Allah-led Yemeni Armed Forces enters its fourth month, developments on the ground indicate that the conflict has reached a critical threshold. However, what Riyadh and its allies could not achieve over the past decade in Yemen seems far from attainable at this point, as Ansar Allah continues to expand its territorial control and target vital Saudi sites. The last week saw a remarkable advance by Ansar Allah towards Aden, the seat of the Yemeni interim government, backed by Saudi Arabia and Western countries. Ansar Allah solidified its hold on the Khor Omairh coastline, west of Aden, and captured parts of Lahij Governorate, encompassing the highland district of Al-Maqatirah. This progress came days after the movement managed to push back Saudi-backed forces from positions overlooking the Bab Al-Mandeb Strait. The consecutive military setbacks in Yemen forced the Mohammad Bin Salman administration to sack the commander of the Saudi coalition’s joint forces, Lieutenant General Fahd al-Salman, and replace him with Saudi Arabia’s chief of general staff, General Fayyad Al-Ruwaili. Overwhelmed by Ansar Allah’s territorial gains during ground clashes, Saudi Arabia intensified its airstrikes across Yemen, with the latest strike on Friday, November 20, targeting Hodeidah port , a major Red Sea maritime harbor. The port was struck despite previous port-for-port retaliation threats by Ansar Allah, after Saudi Arabia had warned of launching the assault hours earlier. The Yemeni Armed Forces spokesperson, Brigadier General Yahya Saree, issued a series of statements vowing that Ansar Allah would target all Saudi ports on the Red Sea should Hodeidah be attacked. “The Armed Forces announce that Jeddah Port and all Saudi enemy ports on the Red Sea coast will be targets for our forces if the enemy carries out its threats to bombard Hodeidah Port,” Saree said. He further cautioned “employees, workers and those present near them to evacuate immediately and stay away.” All shipping companies were also urged “to evacuate their vessels from those ports immediately.” Moreover, the Yemeni Ministry of Electricity and Energy reported on Friday that Saudi warplanes targeted power generation stations in Mocha, Taiz, and in Saadah. In response, Ansar Allah attacked Saudi Arabia’s Al-Shuqaiq power plant and the port of Jazan.
